sections.title: The Coming of the Lord of the Stage

translit: vārīr citampara valli civakāma valli maṇāḷarē vārīr maṇimaṉṟa vāṇarē vārīr.
translation: Please come, oh husband of the goddess Sivakami of Chidambaram, please come! Lord of the jeweled stage, please come!
commentary: The song of invitation begins. Vallalar calls the Lord as the husband of Sivakami, the Divine Mother of Chidambaram, and as the One who dances on the jewelled stage. Each line ends with the same word, "come" (vārīr), and that repeated call carries the whole song.

translit: aruṭperuñ cōtieṉ āṇṭava rētiru ampala vāṇarē vārīr aṉpuṭai yāḷarē vārīr. vārīr
translation: Vast Grace-Light, my Ruler! Sacred Lord of the Stage, please come! You who are filled with love, please come. Please come!
commentary: The invitation names God directly: ArutPerunJothi, his Ruler, Lord of the sacred Ambalam, the One full of love. The call "come, come" is not doubt that God will come. It is the longing of a heart that wants the presence it already knows.

translit: accam tavirtteṉṉai āṭkoṇ ṭaruḷiya antaṇa rēiṅku vārīr ampalat taiyarē vārīr. vārīr
translation: Oh, antaṇar (gracious, cool-natured one) who removed my fear and graciously took me as Your own, please come here! Lord of the sacred stage, please come. Please come!
commentary: Vallalar remembers what God has already done: removed his fear and taken him as God's own. He calls God antaṇar, the gracious one whose nature is coolness and compassion. Because God came before, he calls with confidence for God to come again.

translit: aṉpuru vāṉavar iṉpuṟa uḷḷē aṟivuru vāyiṉīr vārīr aruṭperuñ jōtiyīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: For the delight of those who embody love, You became the form of consciousness within them. Please come! Oh, Vast Grace-Light, please come. Please come!
commentary: For those whose very form is love, God becomes the form of consciousness within them, to their delight. Love and knowing are joined here: where love is, God shines as awareness. Vallalar calls this indwelling Light by its name, ArutPerunJothi, and asks it to come.

translit: aṇṭaṅkaḷ ellām aṇuvil aṭakkum arumperuñ cittarē vārīr aṟputa rēiṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: Oh, rare and great siddhar who contains all the universes within a single atom, please come! Oh, wondrous one, please come here. Please come. Please come!
commentary: God's power is so immense that the entire cosmos can be contained within a single atom, yet this being is also a siddhar (a perfected one) who can be called upon personally. Vallalar begins with the paradox of a God who is both infinitely vast and intimately available.

translit: ammaiyu māyeṉak kappaṉu mākieṉ aṉpaṉu māyiṉīr vārīr aṅkaṇa rēiṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: You became my mother and my father, and my beloved. Come! O Anganar, come here! Come!
commentary: The divine relationship is one of the closest family bonds. By becoming mother, father, and beloved, God fulfills every dimension of human love and care. The name Anganar (the one with gracious eyes) reinforces this image of a loving, attentive presence.

translit: allal aṟutteṉ aṟivai viḷakkiya ampala vāṇarē vārīr aṅkaṇa rēiṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: You who cut away my suffering and illumined my awareness, O Ambalavānar, come! O Anganar, come here! Come!
commentary: God's presence actively removes suffering and awakens inner knowing. Vallalar addresses God as Ambalavānar (the Dancer in the Hall), a name for Siva whose cosmic dance creates and dissolves universes. Here, that same dance is an inner one that brings enlightenment to the soul.

translit: appaṇi poṉmuṭi appaṉeṉ ṟēttumey aṉparuk kaṉparē vārīr iṉpam tara:iṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: O Beloved of the true devotees who praise You as 'Father whose golden crown is adorned with the river,' come! To grant bliss, come here! Come!
commentary: True, heartfelt devotion is the way to attract God, whose very purpose is to grant bliss. The image of the "Father with the serpent on His golden crown" is a classic portrait of Siva, showing that Vallalar's personal path is rooted in a recognizable tradition of worship.

translit: accutar nāṉmukar ucciyil meccum aṭikkama lattīrē vārīr naṭikkaval līriṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: O You whose lotus feet are praised by Achyutan and Nanmugan, who place them upon their heads, come! O masterful Dancer, come here! Come!
commentary: The God that Vallalar invokes is the supreme reality, worshipped even by the other great gods of the Hindu tradition. By stating that Achyutan (Vishnu, the preserver) and Nanmugan (Brahma, the creator) bow to God's feet, he establishes the ultimate authority of the masterful Dancer he calls to come.

translit: aṇṭark karumpatan toṇṭark keḷitil aḷittiṭa vallīrē vārīr kaḷitteṉṉai āṇṭīrē vārīr. vārīr
translation: O You who are able to easily grant Your devotees the state so rare for the celestials, come! You who joyfully took me as Your own, come! Come!
commentary: The highest spiritual states, which are extremely difficult for even celestial beings to attain, are given freely to devoted souls. This is an act of grace, a joyful choice by God to accept and uplift the devotee.

translit: ampara māṉaci tampara nāṭakam āṭaval līriṅku vārīr pāṭalu vantīrēvārīr. vārīr
translation: You who can perform the cosmic dance of Chidambaram, come here! You who delighted in the song, come! Come!
commentary: The dance in Chidambaram (the space of consciousness) represents God's endless, living activity that creates and sustains the universe. By calling God to come and delight in this song of praise, the devotee is asking for that divine, creative presence to enter their own life.

translit: ātia ṉātieṉ ṟāraṇam pōṟṟum arumperuñ jōtiyīr vārīr āṉanta nāṭarē vārīr. vārīr
translation: O rare, great Jothi, praised by the Vedas as the beginning and the beginningless, come! O Lord of the blissful dance, come! Come!
commentary: God is described as the great light, or Jothi, which the ancient scriptures (Vedas) recognize as being without beginning or end. This cosmic, eternal being is also the Lord of the blissful dance, a source of joy and active grace.

translit: ākama vētam aṉēka mukaṅkoṇ ṭaruccikkum pātarē vārīr āruyir nātarē vārīr. vārīr
translation: O One whose feet are worshipped by the Agamas and Vedas in countless ways, come! O Lord of my precious life, come! Come!
commentary: The sacred texts of both the Vedas and the Agamas (scriptures on temple rituals and philosophy) are described as trying to comprehend and worship God from countless different perspectives. Yet beyond all scripture, God is simply the Lord of one's own precious life.

translit: ācaṟum antaṅkaḷ āṟum pukaṉṟanal āriya rēiṅku vārīr āṉantak kūttarē vārīr. vārīr
translation: O noble Teacher who proclaimed the six faultless antas, come here! O blissful Dancer, come! Come!
commentary: The six antas are the six 'ends' or culminations of knowledge: Vedanta, Siddhanta, Bodhanta, Nadanta, Yoganta and Kalanta. God is the Teacher who proclaimed them all, and Vallalar calls this Teacher, the blissful Dancer, to come.

translit: āla niḻaṟkaṇ amarntaṟañ coṉṉanal āriya rēiṅku vārīr āṉantak kūttarē vārīr. vārīr
translation: O noble Teacher who sat in the shade of the banyan tree and taught righteousness, come here! O blissful Dancer, come! Come!
commentary: This verse evokes the classic image of Siva as Dakshinamurti, the youthful teacher who sits in silence under a banyan tree. He imparts profound wisdom to aged sages through his mere presence and silence. God is portrayed as the source of all righteousness, a teacher who can instruct without words.

translit: āramu tākieṉ āviyaik kākkiṉṟa āṉanta rēiṅku vārīr āṭalval līriṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: O rare nectar that protects my very life, O embodiment of bliss, come here. O expert dancer, come here. Come here.
commentary: God is experienced here as a life-sustaining force, a "rare nectar" that doesn't just guard the soul but nourishes and vivifies it from within. This divine presence is the very definition of bliss and the source of the cosmic dance of existence.

translit: ātara vāyeṉ aṟivait teḷivit tamutam aḷittīrē vārīr āṭiya pātarē vārīr. vārīr
translation: You who lovingly clarified my intellect and granted me nectar, come here. O you with the dancing feet, come here. Come here.
commentary: Spiritual awakening involves both the head and the heart. Grace clarifies the mind, removing confusion and doubt, while simultaneously granting the "nectar" of blissful experience. The intellect becomes clear and the soul tastes deep joy, both gifts from the "dancing feet" of the Divine.

translit: ātāra mītāṉat tappālum kāṇṭaṟ karumperuñ jōtiyīr vārīr karumpiṉil iṉikkiṉṟīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: O vast Jothi, so difficult to behold even beyond the planes of the ādhāras, come here. You who are sweeter than sugarcane, come here. Come here.
commentary: The supreme light, Jothi, is not found within the familiar yogic system of ādhāras (the body's subtle energy centers). It exists beyond them, making it almost impossible to reach through conventional practices. Yet, this transcendent reality is also described as intimately sweet and desirable, closer and more pleasing than any earthly taste.

translit: ātiyum antamum illā arumperum jōtiya rēiṅku vārīr vētiya rēiṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: O rare, great Jothi with no beginning and no end, come here. O embodiment of sacred knowledge, come here. Come here.
commentary: The divine light, Jothi, is presented as eternal, existing outside of time, without a beginning or an end. By also calling God Vediyar (embodiment of sacred knowledge), Vallalar identifies this infinite light with ultimate truth and wisdom.

translit: āṭalkoṇ ṭīrtiru vampalat tēeṉṟaṉ pāṭalkoṇ ṭīriṅku vārīr kūṭaval līriṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: You who danced in the Tiru Ampalam and accepted my songs, come here. You who are able to unite with me, come here. Come here.
commentary: The relationship with the divine becomes deeply personal here. Vallalar refers to God dancing in the Tiru Ampalam (the sacred hall of consciousness) and, most importantly, accepting his own songs as a worthy offering. The final plea to unite is the goal of all this devotion: to witness God and to merge with God completely.

translit: ākkam koṭutteṉṟaṉ tūkkam taṭuttaeṉ āṇṭava rēiṅku vārīr tāṇṭava rēiṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: My Lord who gave me prosperity and prevented my sleep, come here. O Dancer, come here. Come.
commentary: God is both the source of all good things and the One who has taken away his sleep. Vallalar means this plainly: the sleep that wastes life has been put away, and with it the slumber of ignorance. Kept awake by God, he calls the Dancer to come.

translit: āpattai nīkkiōr tīpattai ēṟṟieṉ āṇavam pōkkiṉīr vārīr kāṇavan tēṉiṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: You removed danger, lit a lamp, and dispelled my ego; come. I have come to see you; come here. Come.
commentary: God's grace acts in three ways: it protects from worldly harm, illuminates the mind with wisdom, and dissolves the ego. For Vallalar, removing the ego, the core illusion of being a separate self, is the final and most needed step before one can truly "see" and unite with God.

translit: itutaru ṇamtaru ṇamtaru ṇameṉ iṟaiyava rēiṅku vārīr kāṇavan tēṉiṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: This is the moment, the moment, the moment. My God, come here. I have come to see you; come here. Come.
commentary: The repetition of "this is the moment" creates a powerful sense of urgency and imminence. Spiritual realization can happen right now. All the preparation is complete, and the final union is at hand.

translit: iccaiyiṉ vaṇṇam eṉakkaruḷ ceyya itutaru ṇamiṅku vārīr iṉṉamu tāyiṉīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: This is the moment to bestow grace upon me according to my desire; come here. You who became sweet nectar, come. Come.
commentary: The soul's one true desire is for God, and Vallalar declares that the time has come for this desire to be fulfilled. He describes God as "sweet nectar," emphasizing that the divine presence is a deeply felt, blissful experience that nourishes the soul.

translit: iṉpam koṭuttēeṉ tuṉpam keṭuttuḷ irukkiṉṟa nātarē vārīr irukkiṉ poruḷāṉīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: O Lord who dwells within, giving joy and destroying my sorrow, come. You who became the meaning of the Rig Veda, come. Come.
commentary: God is experienced in two fundamental ways: as an intimate presence within, replacing sorrow with joy, and as the ultimate reality that makes up all of existence. The Lord who transforms our inner world is the very substance of the cosmos itself.

translit: iravum pakalum itayatti lūṟi iṉikkum amutarē vārīr iṉittari yēṉiṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: O sweet ambrosia, welling up in my heart night and day, come! I can no longer bear it here; come. Come.
commentary: A constant inner taste of God's sweetness, instead of bringing satisfaction, has created an unbearable pain of separation. The partial experience of the divine makes the continued existence in a world without God's full presence impossible to endure.

translit: iṉṉumtāḻt taṅkē iruppa taḻakaṉṟu itutaru ṇamiṅku vārīr irumaiyum āyiṉīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: To delay and remain there any longer is not right. This is the moment; come here. You who have become both this world and the next, come. Come.
commentary: The speaker's intimacy with God is so close that they can claim it is "not right" for God to delay any further. By calling God "You who have become duality," Vallalar points to the divine as the source of both separation and union, and asks that power to now resolve the division.

translit: iṭartavirt tiṉpam eṉakkaḷit tāḷaṟ kitutaru ṇamiṅku vārīr iṉiyava rēiṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: This is the moment to remove my affliction, grant me bliss, and rule over me. Come here. O sweet one, come here. Come.
commentary: This verse clearly states the desired outcome of God's arrival: to end all affliction, to be filled with bliss, and to live in a state of complete surrender to divine will. The speaker seeks a vision and a total inner transformation.

translit: iṟaiyum poṟuppari teṉṉuyir nātarē ittaru ṇamiṅku vārīr itanaṭañ ceykiṉṟīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: I cannot bear it for even a moment longer, O Lord of my soul! Come here at this very instant. You who perform the benevolent dance, come. Come.
commentary: The urgency reaches its peak, with the speaker declaring they cannot endure separation for even another instant. The "benevolent dance" refers to the cosmic activity of God, which is seen as an expression of grace that the speaker now begs to witness directly.

translit: immaiyi lēeṉak kammaiyiṉ iṉpam itueṉ ṟaḷittīrē vārīr itayat tiruntīrē vārīr. vārīr
translation: You who, in this very life, granted me the bliss of the next, declaring "This is it," come! You who have dwelled in my heart, come. Come.
commentary: The plea is grounded in a past promise. Vallalar recalls a moment when God gave him a direct experience of heavenly bliss while still in this world, showing him it was attainable now. God is an intimate presence who has already resided in his heart, and this memory fuels his desire for that union to be made permanent.

translit: iṅkaṅkeṉ ṉāmalē eḷḷukkuḷ eṇṇeypōl eṅkum niṟaintīrē vārīr inteḻil vaṇṇarē vārīr. vārīr
translation: You fill everything, more than here or there, like oil within a sesame seed. Come. O one of this beautiful form, come. Come.
commentary: This verse uses a classic image to describe God's presence: like oil hidden inside a sesame seed, God pervades every particle of existence. Although intellectually the devotee knows God is everywhere, the heart still yearns for a direct, personal encounter with God's beautiful form. The longing is for the hidden God to reveal himself.

translit: iṇaioṉṟum illā iṇaiyaṭi eṉtalai ēṟavait tīriṅku vārīr iṟutiyi līriṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: You placed your incomparable sacred feet upon my head. Come here. O eternal one, come here. Come.
commentary: Placing the sacred feet upon a devotee's head is the highest symbol of blessing and initiation in Indian spirituality. Vallalar recalls this ultimate act of grace, where God claimed him completely. This memory of divine contact is the basis for his current plea, asking the "eternal one" to make that sacred presence a constant reality.

translit: īṉṟāḷum entaiyum eṉkuru vumeṉak kiṉpamum āyiṉīr vārīr aṉparuk kaṉparē vārīr. vārīr
translation: You became my mother, my father, my guru, and my bliss. Come. O lover of your devotees, come. Come.
commentary: For the devotee, God fulfills every essential relationship. The divine becomes the ultimate source of love, guidance, and joy, replacing the need for any other worldly support.

translit: īṉam aṟuttumeyñ ñāṉa viḷakkeṉ itayattil ēṟṟiṉīr vārīr utayac cuṭariṉīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: Cutting away my flaws, you lit the lamp of true wisdom in my heart. Come. O dawning flame, come. Come.
commentary: Spiritual transformation involves two divine actions: the removal of inner flaws and the ignition of inner wisdom. The image of the "dawning flame" portrays enlightenment as a living, growing light within the heart.

translit: īṭaṟi yātamey vīṭutan taṉparai iṉpuṟac ceykiṉṟīr vārīr vaṉpark kariyīrē vārīr. vārīr
translation: Giving the incomparable true home, you make your devotees blissful. Come. O one inaccessible to the hard-hearted, come. Come.
commentary: The ultimate state of liberation, the "true home," is a gift of grace, not a reward for effort. This verse makes it clear that the sole condition for receiving this gift is an open and loving heart; it is withheld from those who are closed and hard-hearted.

translit: ītiyal eṉṟuniṉ ṟōtiya vētattiṟ keṭṭā tiruntīrē vārīr naṭṭārk keḷiyīrē vārīr. vārīr
translation: You remained unattainable to the Vedas that stood and proclaimed, "This is its nature." Come here. You who are accessible to Your friends, come here. Come here.
commentary: The most sacred scriptures could not fully grasp or define God, yet the divine is easily known through a direct, loving friendship. This places the personal experience of love far above intellectual knowledge or scriptural authority as the true path to God.

translit: īcar eṉumpala tēcarkaḷ pōṟṟumna ṭēcarē nīriṅku vārīr nēcarē nīriṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: O Natēsar, praised by the many gods known as 'Īsar'! You, come here. O beloved one, You, come here. Come here.
commentary: Even other great gods, called Īsar (Lords), worship Siva as the supreme Cosmic Dancer, Natēsar. Yet for the devotee, this highest of beings is simply a beloved friend (nēcar).

translit: īcar palikkuḻalnēcareṉ ṟaṉparkaḷ ēcaniṉ ṟīriṅku vārīr nācamil līriṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: You stood while devotees reproached you, calling you "The Lord who loves to wander for alms." Come here. You who are indestructible, come here. Come here.
commentary: The relationship with God can be so intimate that devotees feel free to lovingly tease Him, alluding to stories of Siva appearing as a wandering beggar. This playful closeness does not diminish God's true nature as the eternal, indestructible reality.

translit: īṟaṟi yāmaṟai yōṉeṉ ṟaṟiñar iyampaniṉ ṟīriṅku vārīr vayantaru vīriṅku vārīr vārīr
translation: You stood while the wise declared, "He is the one whose end the Vedas do not know." Come here. You who grant vitality, come here. Come here.
commentary: The ancient Vedas and the wisest sages declare that God is infinite, without beginning or end. Vallalar connects this mystery to our own lives: this same limitless being is the direct source of our vitality and strength.

translit: ītalkaṇ ṭēmikak kātalkoṇ ṭēṉeṉak kītalcey vīriṅku vārīr ōtari yīriṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: I have fallen deeply in love, witnessing Your generosity. You who will be generous to me, come here. You who are beyond all description, come here. Come here.
commentary: Devotion is born from witnessing God's boundless generosity. Seeing this grace extended to others inspires a deep love in the speaker, who now confidently asks for that same generosity to be shown to them.

translit: īṭaṇai aṟṟaneñ cūṭaṇai uṟṟumaṟ ṟīṭaṇai yīriṅku vārīr āṭaval līriṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: You who entered and united with my peerless heart, You who are without equal, come here. You who are able to dance, come here. Come here. Come. Come.
commentary: This verse expresses a beautiful tension in the spiritual path. The divine has already entered and merged with the speaker's innermost self, yet there is still a passionate call for God to appear more fully and actively, symbolized here as the cosmic dancer.

translit: īṇṭaṟi vōṅkiṭat tūṇṭaṟi vākiuḷ īṇṭukiṉ ṟīriṅku vārīr āṇṭava rēiṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: So that knowledge may flourish here, you become the instigating wisdom and abound within. Come here. O Master, come here. Come here. Come. Come.
commentary: True spiritual understanding is not something we achieve on our own. It begins when a divine wisdom enters and acts from within, both sparking the initial insight and becoming the very knowledge that grows inside us.

translit: uḷḷatē uḷḷatu viḷḷatu veṉṟeṉak kuḷḷa turaiceytīr vārīr vaḷḷal viraintiṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: You declared to me what is real, stating, "That which exists is the only existence." Come. O benefactor, come here quickly. Come. Come.
commentary: This verse contains a core teaching received directly by the speaker: reality is one. The simple truth, "That which exists is the only existence," points to a singular, unified reality where all distinctions dissolve into one Being.

translit: uruvāy aruvāy uruvaru vāyavai oṉṟumal līriṅku vārīr eṉṟumnal līriṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: You are form, formlessness, and form-and-formlessness, yet you are none of these. Come here. You who are forever good, come here. Come here. Come. Come.
commentary: God can be experienced in any way imaginable: with a specific form, as pure formlessness, or as a state combining both. Yet, the divine is not limited by any of these descriptions. God's ultimate nature transcends every category we might try to place it in.

translit: uṟavum pakaiyum uṭaiya naṭaiyil uṟavumeṇ ṇēṉiṅku vārīr piṟavunaṇ ṇēṉiṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: In the way of the world with its kinships and enmities, I do not consider even kinship. Come here. I do not draw near to anything else. Come here. Come. Come.
commentary: The singular focus on God has caused all worldly distinctions, like friend and foe or even family bonds, to fade in importance. This states a priority, with no rejection of people: the relationship with the Divine has become the only one that truly matters.

translit: uḷḷak karuttaināṉ vaḷḷaṟ kuraippateṉ uḷḷat tiruntīrē vārīr viḷḷaṟ kariyīrē vārīr. vārīr
translation: Why should I tell my heart's thoughts to the generous Lord? You are already in my heart, come here. You who are indescribable, come here. Come here.
commentary: There is no need to articulate prayers or requests, because God already dwells within the heart and knows its deepest feelings. This expresses a deep intimacy, where the separation between the devotee and the Divine has dissolved.

translit: uyyaval lārkkaruḷ ceyyaval līrnāṉum uyyaval lēṉiṅku vārīr ceyyaval līriṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: You who can grant grace to those able to be saved, I too am able to be saved. Come here. You who are capable, come here. Come here.
commentary: A shift in consciousness has occurred: the speaker now sees themself as worthy of receiving God's grace. This is a humble recognition that the capacity for salvation, which God grants, is now present within them.

translit: uṭaiyava rārik kaṭaiyava ṉēṉuk kuṭaiyava rēiṅku vārīr caṭaiyava rēiṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: Who is the master for me, this lowly one? You are the master, come here. O one with matted locks, come here. Come here.
commentary: In a moment of deep humility, the speaker asks who could possibly be the master for someone so "lowly." The answer is immediate: only God can be. The reference to "matted locks" is a traditional way of invoking Lord Siva, who is often depicted this way as a great ascetic.

translit: uṟaṅki iṟaṅkum ulakavar pōlanāṉ uṟaṅkamāṭ ṭēṉiṅku vārīr iṟaṅkamāṭ ṭēṉiṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: I will not sleep and perish like the people of the world, come here. I will not perish, come here. Come here.
commentary: Worldly people sleep, and sleeping they go down into death. Vallalar declares that he will not sleep as they do and will not die as they do; he holds to the wakefulness that belongs to the deathless life.

translit: uṇṭuṭut tiṉṉum uḻalamāṭ ṭēṉamu tuṇṭi virumpiṉēṉ vārīr uṇṭi tara:iṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: I cannot wander about, merely eating and dressing. I desire to consume ambrosia, come here. Come here to give me that food. Come here.
commentary: The routines of daily life, like eating and dressing, have become empty and meaningless to the speaker. The only nourishment he now seeks is the "ambrosia" of divine grace, a spiritual food that grants eternal life.

translit: uṉṉutō ṟuṉṉutō ṟuḷḷē iṉikkiṉṟa uttama rēiṅku vārīr uṟṟa tuṇaiyāṉīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: O perfect one who sweetens me within each time I think of you, come here. You have become my true companion. Come. Come.
commentary: This verse describes the inner experience of devotion. The thought of God is a tangible sweetness felt within the self. This intimacy transforms God from a distant, powerful being into a constant, personal companion.

translit: ummāṇai ummāṇai ummaial lāleṉak kuṟṟavar maṟṟilai vārīr uṟṟaṟin tīriṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: I swear on you, I swear on you, I have no one else close to me but you. Come. You know this intimately. Come here. Come. Come.
commentary: The repeated oath conveys an urgent and total sincerity. It is a vow of absolute reliance, a declaration that God is the only true relation he has. He appeals to God's own intimate knowledge, stating that God already knows this to be true.

translit: ūṉa naṭantavirt tāṉa naṭaṅkāṭṭu mōṉa naṭēcarē vārīr ñāṉa naṭēcarē vārīr. vārīr
translation: O Lord of the silent dance who stops the flawed dance and shows the true dance, come. O Lord of the wisdom dance, come. Come. Come.
commentary: The 'flawed dance' is the restless, ego-driven activity of ordinary life. Vallalar asks God, as the Lord of the silent dance (Mōna Naṭēcar), to replace this with the silent, perfect motion of pure wisdom (jñānam). This is about transforming the very nature of one's inner activity from chaotic to divine.

translit: ūrumil līroru pērumil līraṟi vōrumil līriṅku vārīr yārumil līriṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: You have no town, you have no name, you have no one who truly knows you. Come here. You are without kin. Come here. Come. Come.
commentary: God is utterly free from the identities that define human life: a place of origin, a name, a family, or even being known or understood by others. By pointing this out, Vallalar highlights the absolute, unconditioned nature of the divine, which cannot be pinned down by any label or relationship.

translit: ūṟu civāṉantap pēṟu tarukiṉṟa vīṟuṭai yīriṅku vārīr nīṟuṭai yīriṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: O eminent one who gives the gift of the ever-springing bliss of Siva, come here. O you who wear the sacred ash, come here. Come. Come.
commentary: This verse connects the nameless, formless being of the previous verse with recognizable attributes of the god Siva. The sacred ash (nīṟu) is a traditional symbol of purity, detachment, and divine power. God is both the source of unending bliss and the one who embodies these sacred signs.

translit: ūṉṟunum cēvaṭi cāṉṟu tarikkilēṉ ēṉṟukoḷ vīriṅku vārīr āṉṟava rēiṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: I cannot bear the imprint of your planted, sacred feet. You who will accept me, come here. O perfected one, come here. Come.
commentary: To receive the touch of a deity's feet is a great blessing, but the speaker feels too frail and unworthy to even bear their imprint. This is an expression of deep humility, paired with the faith that God, the "perfected one," will accept him regardless of his weakness.

translit: ūṟṟai uṭampitu māṟṟuyar poṉṉeṉa ēṟṟam aruḷceyvīr vārīr tēṟṟam aruḷceyvīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: You who will graciously make this body of secretions eminent, like gold of high purity, come. You who will graciously grant clarity, come. Come.
commentary: This verse captures a central hope in Vallalar's path: the transformation of the physical body. He describes the body in its raw, messy reality as a "body of secretions" and asks God to alchemically change it into something pure, lasting, and radiant, like gold. This is a plea for physical perfection and the spiritual clarity that it enables.

translit: ūṭalil līreṉaik kūṭalval līreṉṉuḷ pāṭalcol vīriṅku vārīr āṭalnal līriṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: You who are without lover's quarrels, you who are skilled in uniting with me, you who speak songs within me, come here. O masterful dancer, come here. Come.
commentary: The relationship with God is presented as a perfect union, free from the conflicts and misunderstandings of human love. God is an intimate partner who is "skilled in uniting" with the soul and an inner voice that inspires song. The call to the "masterful dancer" evokes the divine as the source of all cosmic rhythm and activity.

translit: ūkkam koṭutteṉṟaṉ ēkkam keṭuttaruḷ ākka maṭuttīrē vārīr tūkkam tavirttīrē vārīr. vārīr
translation: You who gave me zeal, destroyed my pining, and bestowed the wealth of grace, come. You who have ended my slumber, come. Come.
commentary: This is a song of gratitude for a spiritual awakening. The speaker acknowledges that God has already replaced desperate longing with spiritual energy and the "wealth of grace." To be awakened from "slumber" is to be brought out of a state of spiritual ignorance into a new, living awareness.

translit: ūmai eḻuttiṉuḷ āmai eḻuttuṇṭeṉ ṟōmai aṟivittīr vārīr cēmañ ceṟivittīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: You who taught the nature of Ōm, declaring that the tortoise letter is within the mute letter, come. You who bestowed abundant security, come. Come.
commentary: God is the inner teacher who reveals the deepest spiritual secrets. Here, Vallalar refers to the sacred syllable Ōm, where the "mute letter" is 'A' (the primal sound) and the "tortoise letter" is 'U' (the preserving sound it contains). This revelation of the structure of reality brings a deep sense of security and peace.

translit: ūka milēṉpeṟṟa tēkam aḻiyāta yōkam koṭuttīrē vārīr pōkam koṭuttīrē vārīr. vārīr
translation: You gave the yoga that makes imperishable the body I received, I who am without reasoning. Come! You gave blissful experience. Come! Come!
commentary: Even for one who feels unworthy and unenlightened, grace can grant the ultimate gift: a spiritual practice, or yoga, that makes the physical body itself immortal. Most spiritual paths aim to escape the body; Vallalar's path, given by God, aims to perfect it into an imperishable vessel for blissful experience.

translit: ūtiyam tantanal vētiya rēuṇmai ōtiya nātarē vārīr ātia ṉātiyīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: O great sage who gave me my true reward, O Lord who taught the truth, come! O You who are the beginning and without beginning, come! Come!
commentary: The true reward of a spiritual life is the gift of truth from God. God is presented as both the ultimate source of everything, existing before any beginning, and the personal teacher who makes that ultimate reality known.

translit: eṉkuṟai tīrtteṉṉuḷ naṉkuṟai vīriṉi eṉkuṟai eṉmuṉṉīr vārīr taṉkuṟai illīrē vārīr. vārīr
translation: You ended my flaws and reside fully within me; now that You are before me, what lack do I have? Come! O You who are Yourself without flaw, come! Come!
commentary: By filling the soul, God removes all of its flaws and imperfections. In the divine presence, there is a feeling of absolute completeness, a state where nothing is lacking because God, who lacks nothing, has become one's all.

translit: eṉṉuyir ākieṉ ṟaṉuyirk kuḷḷēōr iṉṉuyir āyiṉīr vārīr eṉṉuyir nātarē vārīr. vārīr
translation: Becoming my very life, You became a sweet, inner life within my soul. Come! O Lord of my life, come! Come!
commentary: God's presence is the very life force animating our own soul. This verse describes a deep intimacy, where the distinction between the devotee's life and the divine life dissolves into a single, sweet, loving union.

translit: eṉkaṇ aruḷceyteṉ puṉkaṇ vilakkiya eṉkaṇ ṇaṉaiyīrē vārīr eṉkaṇ ṇutalīrē vārīr. vārīr
translation: You graced me and removed my misery, O You who are like my own eye. Come! O You with the eye on Your forehead, come! Come!
commentary: God is both the inner lens through which we perceive reality and the transcendent power that purifies our vision. Likening God to our own eye suggests the divine is essential for all understanding, while the reference to the forehead eye (a classic attribute of Lord Siva) points to the power that destroys illusion.

translit: ellā uyirkaḷum nallār eṉattoḻum ellāmval līriṅku vārīr collā nilaiyiṉīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: You are the all-powerful one, whom all living beings worship, calling you the Good One. Come here. You who are in a state beyond words, come. Come.
commentary: The impulse to worship a single, benevolent, and all-powerful reality is universal to all life, even if that reality can never be fully described in words. Vallalar sees a common spiritual instinct in all beings to revere what is good, pointing to a truth that transcends any single religion or philosophy.

translit: eṭṭum iraṇṭumeṉ ṟiṭṭu vaḻaṅkutal eṭṭum paṭiceytīr vārīr eṭṭuru vāyiṉīr vārīr.vārīr
translation: You made attainable that which is spoken of as 'eight and two'. Come. You who became the eight forms, come. Come.
commentary: The highest spiritual goals, often discussed as abstract concepts, are made real and attainable through God's grace. The "eight and two" refers to the sacred syllable Aum, representing ultimate reality, while the "eight forms" refers to God's manifestation as the entire cosmos. For Vallalar, these are ideas to be studied and a living presence to be experienced.

translit: eṉṟu kaṇṭāyitunaṉṟukoṇ ṭāḷuka eṉṟutan tīriṅku vārīr aṉṟuvan tīriṉṟu vārīr. vārīr
translation: You gave this to me, saying, "You have seen it. This is good; take it and possess it." Come here. You who came then, come now. Come. Come.
commentary: This verse describes the moment of spiritual realization as a direct gift and a command from God. The plea for God to 'come now' as he 'came then' is the soul's deep longing to turn that peak experience into a constant, abiding presence.

translit: eccama yaṅkaḷum poyccama yameṉṟīr iccama yamiṅku vārīr meyccama yantantīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: You declared every religion a false religion. At this time, come here. You gave the true religion. Come. Come.
commentary: Vallalar reports plainly what God has done: declared the other religions false and given him the true religion (meyccamayam). He does not argue the point; he states what was revealed to him. Elsewhere in the Sixth Thirumurai he names this true path Suddha Sanmarkkam. Having received it, he calls God to come now.

translit: eṉpāṟ kaḷippoṭum aṉpāloṉ ṟīntitai iṉpāl peṟukiṉṟīr vārīr teṉpāl mukaṅkoṇṭīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: With joy and love you bestowed the One Thing upon me, and in turn, you receive it with sweetness. Come. You who have a south-facing form, come. Come.
commentary: The relationship with God is a joyful, mutual exchange. God gives the soul the 'One Thing', the singular experience of divine union, and in turn receives the soul's loving acceptance as a sweet gift. The 'south-facing form' refers to God as Dakshinamurti, the silent teacher who imparts ultimate wisdom.

translit: ecca uraiyaṉṟeṉ iccaiel lāmuma ticcaikaṇ ṭīriṅku vārīr accamta virttīrē vārīr. vārīr
translation: This is no leftover talk; all my desire is Your desire, you see. Come here. You who have removed my fear, come. Come.
commentary: This state of union is so complete that the poet's own will has been replaced by the divine will. His words are not empty talk; they express this new reality, in which personal desire has dissolved into God's desire. Because there is no longer a separate self to protect, all fear has vanished.

translit: eṇṇamel lāmuma teṇṇamal lālvēṟōr eṇṇam eṉakkillai vārīr vaṇṇam aḷikkiṉṟīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: All my thoughts are Your thoughts, and I have no other thought besides. Come. You who bestow splendor, come. Come.
commentary: Following the alignment of will in the previous verse, the poet's mind itself has now become one with God. His thoughts are no longer generated by his limited self, but are a direct reflection of divine consciousness. This is the culmination of devotion: the small, separate self dissolves its thinking into the infinite mind of God.

translit: ērāya nāṉmukar nārāya ṇarmaṟṟum pārāya ṇamceyvīr vārīr ūrāyam āyiṉīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: You are the one whom the dignified Four-Faced One, Narayana, and others continuously praise. Come. You have become the talk of the town, come. Come.
commentary: The God that Vallalar addresses is the supreme reality, worshipped even by other great gods like Brahma (the Four-Faced One) and Vishnu (Narayana). Yet, in a beautiful turn of phrase, he says this cosmic Lord has become the "talk of the town," suggesting that the highest, most distant truth has become a living, personal, and celebrated reality here and now.

translit: ēma mikuntiru vāma cukantarum ēma capēcarē vārīr cōma cikāmaṇi vārīr. vārīr
translation: O Lord of the Golden Hall, who with great love grant the bliss of the beautiful left side, come. O crest-jewel with the moon, come. Come.
commentary: This verse invokes God using classic imagery of Siva. The "Lord of the Golden Hall" refers to Siva as Nataraja, the cosmic dancer at the great temple of Chidambaram. The "bliss of the beautiful left side" signifies the grace of the Goddess, his consort, who represents divine energy and is inseparable from him.

translit: ēta milāppara nāta muṭipporuḷ ētatu colluvīr vārīr ītal uṭaiyīrē vārīr. vārīr
translation: You who will tell me what that is, the flawless ultimate reality of Para Natham, come. You who possess such generosity, come. Come.
commentary: The poet asks God to reveal the ultimate secret of existence, which he calls Para Nātham (the supreme, transcendental sound). In this tradition, the universe itself originates from a primordial vibration, and to understand it is to understand reality itself. This is a plea for the highest knowledge, which only God, in his generosity, can grant.

translit: ēka parāpara yōka veḷikkappāl ēka veḷiniṉṟīr vārīr ēkar aṉēkarē vārīr. vārīr
translation: You stood in the singular space, beyond the space of the one supreme yoga; come. You who are one and many, come. Come.
commentary: God exists in a state of pure oneness that is even beyond the highest states achieved through spiritual practices like yoga. The verse points to a reality that transcends all disciplines and concepts. Yet, this absolute unity also manifests as the entire multiplicity of the universe, embodying the paradox of being both one and many at the same time.

translit: ēṟi iṟaṅki iruntēṉ iṟaṅkāmal ēṟavait tīriṅku vārīr tēṟavait tīriṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: I was constantly rising and falling; you made me ascend without descending. Come here. You brought me to clarity. Come here. Come.
commentary: The spiritual path is often an unstable cycle of progress and relapse, of rising with insight and falling back into old patterns. Vallalar celebrates a moment of divine grace that broke this cycle, transforming his struggle into a permanent, stable ascent and bringing him a lasting state of clarity.

translit: ēkānta naṉṉilai yōkāntat tuḷḷateṉ ṟēkāntam colliṉīr vārīr tēkāntam illīrē vārīr. vārīr
translation: You told me in private that the good state of oneness is within the culmination of yoga; come. You who have no bodily end, come. Come.
commentary: The ultimate state of oneness, ekāntam, is an experience found at the very peak of yoga. Vallalar presents this as a secret revealed to him personally by God. By addressing God as one "who has no bodily end," he contrasts the transient human body with the eternal nature of both the divine teacher and the timeless truth being taught.

translit: ēkāta kalvitāṉ cākāta kalviyeṉ ṟēkāta lāṟcoṉṉīr vārīr vēkāta kāliṉīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: With singular love, you told me that the learning which never leaves is the deathless learning; come. You who are the unburning Kāl (vēkāk kāl, the vital air that does not burn), come. Come.
commentary: Most knowledge is temporary and forgotten, but the one truly essential teaching is the 'deathless learning' (sākāta kalvi), the knowledge of how to overcome death. Once attained, it is never lost. God is addressed as the 'unburning Kāl' (vēkāk kāl), the vital air that does not burn away, which Vallalar names among the marks of the deathless state.

translit: ēṭā yirameṉṉai kōṭā moḻioṉṟē ēṭāeṉ ṟīriṅku vārīr īṭāvār illīrē vārīr. vārīr
translation: You said, "What are a thousand manuscripts? A single, unbending word is the true manuscript." Come here. You who have no equal, come. Come.
commentary: Vallalar contrasts the value of extensive scriptural study with direct experience. A single, unbending word of truth received directly from God is the "true manuscript," rendering thousands of physical books secondary. This places inner revelation above all external learning.

translit: ēcāta tantiram pēcāta mantiram īcāṉa mēleṉṟīr vārīr ācāti illīrē vārīr. vārīr
translation: You said the unspoken mantra and the flawless spiritual method are supreme, above even Ishana. Come. You who are without beginning, come. Come.
commentary: The highest spiritual practice is a state of deep silence, beyond any chanted prayer (mantra). This silent method is described as being supreme, transcending even the cosmic powers of Ishana, a traditional name for a high aspect of Siva. The final path is an unspoken, internal one.

translit: ēṉeṉpār vēṟilai nāṉaṉpāṟ kūvukiṉ ṟēṉeṉpāl ēṉeṉpīr vārīr āṉiṉpāl āṭuvīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: There is no one else to answer me. I am calling out of love; answer me, come. You who bathe in cow's milk, come. Come.
commentary: Vallalar calls out of pure love and says there is no one else who will answer him. Only God can answer this call, so he asks God to respond and come. The image of the deity bathing in cow's milk is a familiar reference to temple worship of Siva.

translit: aintu malaṅkaḷum ventu viḻaeḻut taintuñ ceyumeṉṟīr vārīr intu cikāmaṇi vārīr. vārīr
translation: You said the five letters will cause the five impurities to be burned up and fall away. Come. O crest-jewel who wears the moon, come. Come.
commentary: The "five letters" refer to the sacred mantra of Siva, Na Ma Si Va Ya. God has promised Vallalar that repeating this mantra will burn away the five impurities (malams), the layers of ignorance, ego, and karma that bind the soul. This is a practical instruction: a specific sound is given as the key to liberation. But the final mantra that God gave to Ramalinga was the Mahamantra: Arutperunjothi Arutperunjothi, Thanipperunkarunai Arutperunjothi.

translit: aiyamuṟ ṟēṉaiiv vaiyaṅ kariyāka aiyam tavirttīrē vārīr meyyam palattīrē vārīr. vārīr
translation: With the world as a witness, you dispelled the doubt of me, who was so full of doubt. Come. You of the Hall of Truth, come. Come.
commentary: After a period of deep uncertainty, Vallalar celebrates a moment of absolute clarity. God removed his doubt so completely and powerfully that it felt like a public vindication, as if proven "with the world as a witness." This grace comes from the Lord of the "Hall of Truth," the ultimate reality itself.

translit: aiyar naṭampuri meyyareṉ ṟēuṇarn taiyar toḻaniṉṟīr vārīr tuyyar uḷaniṉṟīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: The venerable ones worship you as you stand, realizing you are the Truth who performs the Master's dance. Come. You who dwell in the hearts of the pure, come. Come.
commentary: The most revered sages and spiritual masters all come to the same conclusion: they worship God as the ultimate Truth, the one who performs the cosmic dance of existence. Vallalar affirms that his personal longing leads to the same reality sought by the wise, a reality that dwells in the hearts of the pure.

translit: aivaṇaṅ kāṭṭunum meyvaṇam vēṭṭuniṉ ṟaivaṇar ēttuvīr vārīr poyvaṇam pōkkuvīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: Come, you who are praised by the five great gods, who stand in adoration, desiring your true form which you reveal in five aspects. Come, you who dispel the nature of falsehood. Come.
commentary: God's greatness is such that even the five major deities who govern the cosmos stand in adoration of Him. These cosmic powers themselves long to see His true form. This establishes God as the ultimate reality, beyond all other gods and functions, and as the one who can free the soul from all that is false.

translit: oṉṟē civamatai oṉṟucaṉ mārkkamum oṉṟēeṉ ṟīriṅku vārīr naṉṟēniṉ ṟīriṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: You declared, "Sivam is One, and the Sanmarkkam that unites with It is also one." Come here. You who are firmly established in goodness, come here. Come.
commentary: There is only one ultimate reality, which is called Sivam, and there is only one true path to realize it, the Sanmarkkam. This path is the single way that leads directly to the one God, who is goodness itself.

translit: oppāril līrumak kippāril piḷḷaināṉ oppāri allakāṇ vārīr muppāḻ kaṭantīrē vārīr. vārīr
translation: You are without equal. I am your child in this world; see, this is not an oppāri. Come. You who have crossed the Mūppāḻ, come. Come.
commentary: Vallalar speaks to God with intimate vulnerability, declaring himself a child crying out for his parent. He clarifies that his song is not an oppāri (a funeral lament for something lost) but a plea for union. He addresses God as the one who exists beyond the Mūppāḻ (the three great voids), the ultimate states of nothingness that the soul must transcend.

translit: otta iṭantaṉṉil nittirai ceyeṉṟīr otta iṭaṅkāṭṭa vārīr citta cikāmaṇi vārīr. vārīr
translation: You said, "Sleep in the harmonious place." Come and show me that harmonious place. O Citta Cikāmaṇi, come. Come.
commentary: God has given the instruction to "sleep in the harmonious place," meaning to find rest in a state of perfect inner balance and union. Vallalar now asks God to show him exactly what and where this place of perfect stillness is. He calls God the Citta Cikāmaṇi (Crest-jewel of consciousness), acknowledging that only the highest consciousness can reveal this ultimate state of rest.

translit: oṭṭumaṟ ṟillaināṉ viṭṭup pirikalēṉ oṭṭuvait tēṉummēl vārīr eṭṭuk kuṇattīrē vārīr. vārīr
translation: I have no other attachment; I will not leave and be separated from you. I have fixed my bond on you; come. O you of eight qualities, come. Come.
commentary: In a statement of absolute devotion, Vallalar declares that he has no attachment other than God and will never be separated. He has fixed his whole bond on God alone, and so he calls God to come. He addresses God as the possessor of the classic eight divine qualities (eṭṭuk kuṇam), which include supreme grace and boundless compassion.

translit: orumai nilaiyil irumaiyum tanta orumaiyi ṉīriṅku vārīr perumaiyi ṉīriṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: You who are Oneness, who from a state of unity gave both realms, come here. You who are Greatness, come here. Come.
commentary: God is the ultimate Oneness from which all duality, such as the spiritual and material realms, emerges. Vallalar acknowledges that even though we experience a world of separation, it all originates from a single, unified source.

translit: oṇmai virumpiṉēṉ aṇmaiyil īkuvīr uṇmaicoṉ ṉēṉiṅku vārīr peṇmaiiṭaṅkoṇṭīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: I desired radiance; you will grant it soon. I have spoken the truth, come here. You who have a woman as your left half, come. Come.
commentary: The "radiance" Vallalar seeks is spiritual light and divine grace, and he expresses his certainty that it will be granted. He calls on God in the form that unites masculine and feminine principles, the Lord who is inseparable from his divine energy or consort.

translit: ōṅkāra nāṭakam pāṅkākacceykiṉṟa ōṅkāra nāṭarē vārīr āṅkāra nīkkiṉīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: O Lord of Omkara, who skillfully performs the drama of Omkara, come. You who removed my ego, come. Come.
commentary: Creation is seen as a great cosmic play that unfolds from Omkara, the primordial sound 'Om'. Vallalar addresses God as the director and performer of this universal drama, who also works on a personal level to remove the devotee's ego.

translit: ōṅkumpiṇ ṭāṇṭaṅkaḷ tāṅkum peruveḷi ōṅku naṭēcarē vārīr pāṅkucey vīriṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: O exalted Natesar, you are the great space that supports the rising macrocosms and microcosms. Come. You who will set things right, come here. Come.
commentary: God is the vast, conscious space that contains and supports all existence, from the entire universe (macrocosm) down to the individual being (microcosm). Vallalar addresses Natesar, the Lord of the Cosmic Dance, expressing his faith that this divine presence will resolve his struggles and make everything right.

translit: ōcaiyiṉ uḷḷēōr ācaiutikkamel ōcaicey vittīrē vārīr pācam aṟuttīrē vārīr. vārīr
translation: You made a subtle sound, causing a desire to rise up within it. Come. You who severed my bonds, come. Come.
commentary: The very first spark of desire for God is a subtle sound, a call, that God himself places within the soul. This initial awakening, a gift of grace, is what begins the process of severing the worldly attachments (pācam) that bind us.

translit: ōrā tulakiṉaip pārā tiruniṉak kōrā vakaieṉṟīr vārīr pērā nilaitantīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: You told me, in a way I cannot comprehend, "Do not contemplate or look at the world." Come. You gave me an unchanging state. Come. Come.
commentary: God's guidance can come as a direct, internal command to withdraw attention from the external world. This instruction is a mystical event that leads the soul to an unshakable inner stillness, a state of being that no longer depends on the changing world.

translit: ōṭātu māyaiyai nāṭātu naṉṉeṟi ūṭā tirueṉṟīr vārīr vāṭā tirueṉṟīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: You said, "Do not run after Māyā, do not seek it, and do not obstruct the good path." Come. You said, "Be without withering." Come. Come.
commentary: The divine instruction is clear: stop pursuing Māyā (the illusion of the material world) and do not stray from the true spiritual path. The reward for this focus is a state of being "without withering", a timeless vitality of the soul that is no longer subject to the decay and exhaustion of worldly life.

translit: ōlak kapāṭattaic cālat tiṟantaruḷ ōlakkaṅ kāṭṭiṉīr vārīr kālak kaṇakkillīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: Completely opening the door to the royal court, you showed me the royal court of grace. Come. You who are beyond the reckoning of time, come. Come.
commentary: The "royal court of grace" is a powerful metaphor for a direct and intimate experience of the divine. Vallalar is describing a moment when God revealed His presence completely, as a reality to be entered. This experience of grace comes from a being who is itself beyond all time.

translit: ōṭattiṉ niṉṟoru māṭattil ēṟṟimey yūṭattaik kāṭṭiṉīr vārīr vēṭattaip pūṭṭiṉīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: Lifting me from a boat and placing me in a mansion, you showed me the true body. Come. You fastened this guise upon me. Come. Come.
commentary: The soul's way is depicted here as being lifted from a fragile "boat," representing our unstable worldly life, and placed in a secure "mansion," a state of spiritual permanence. In this higher state of being, God reveals the soul's "true body," its perfected and eternal form, distinct from the temporary physical "guise" we wear in this life.

translit: ōmatti lēnaṭuc cāmatti lēeṉai ōmattaṉākkiṉīr vārīr cāmattanīkkiṉīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: In the fire sacrifice, at midnight, you made me one with the sacrifice itself. Come. You removed death. Come. Come.
commentary: The ōmam, or fire sacrifice, becomes a metaphor for an inner transformation. Vallalar describes a mystical experience where he himself becomes the offering, completely surrendering his individual self into the divine fire. In this ultimate act of devotion, the boundaries dissolve, and the state of deathlessness is achieved.

translit: ōmeṉpa taṟkumuṉ āmeṉ ṟuraittuṭaṉ ūmeṉṟukāṭṭiṉīr vārīr nāmeṉṟu nāṭṭiṉīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: Before I could even say 'Om', you affirmed 'Yes' and showed me the silent 'Ūm'. Come here. You established us as 'We'. Come here. Come here.
commentary: This verse captures the immediacy of divine grace. Before the seeker can even utter the sacred sound 'Om', God has already responded 'Yes'. Grace then reveals the silent source of that sound, represented by 'Ūm', pointing to the unmanifest reality behind all creation. This culminates in the ultimate realization of 'We', a state where the separation between the soul and God dissolves into perfect union.

translit: auviya mārkkattiṉ vevviyal nīkkiyē cevviyaṉ ākkiṉīr vārīr ovvioṉ ṟākkiṉīr vārīr. vārīr
translation: You removed the cruel nature of the path of envy and made me righteous. Come here. You joined with me harmoniously and made us one. Come here. Come here.
commentary: The path to God requires a pure heart. Vallalar credits the divine for removing his inner flaws, specifically the poison of envy (a͠uvviyam), which separates people from each other and from God. Once this negativity was cleared, he was made righteous, creating the inner harmony needed for God to join with him and make them one.

translit: kaṇṇaṉai yīrummaik kāṇaeṉ ācai kaṭalpoṅku kiṉṟatu vārīr uṭaltaṅku kiṉṟatu vārīr. vārīr
translation: O you who are dear as my own eyes, my desire to see you surges like the ocean. Come here. My life lingers on in this body. Come here. Come here.
commentary: The poet's longing for God has become a powerful, uncontrollable force, like a surging ocean. He feels his very life is just lingering in his body, its sole purpose being to wait for the moment of seeing and uniting with the Divine. The physical world feels like a temporary holding place.

translit: kaṇṭaṇain tālaṉṟik kātal aṭaṅkāteṉ kaṇmaṇi yīriṅku vārīr uṇmaṇi yīriṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: This love will not subside unless I see and embrace you. O jewel of my eye, come here. O inner gem, come here. Come here.
commentary: This intense spiritual love cannot be calmed by thoughts or promises; only a direct, tangible union will satisfy it. Vallalar addresses God with intimate names: ‘jewel of my eye’ (kaṇmaṇi), meaning God is his most precious sight, and ‘inner gem’ (uṇmaṇi), acknowledging God as the treasure within his own being.

translit: kaṭṭikkoṇ ṭummaik kalantu koḷalvēṇṭum kāraṇa rēiṅku vārīr pūraṇa rēiṅku vārīr. vārīr
translation: I must embrace you and merge with you. O Primal Cause, come here. O perfect Fullness, come here. Come here.
commentary: The desire for God goes beyond seeing or being near; it is a need to embrace and merge completely, dissolving all separation. Vallalar calls God the ‘Primal Cause’ (Kāraṇar), the source of all existence, and ‘perfect Fullness’ (Pūraṇar), the wholeness that alone can complete the soul.

translit: vārīr citampara valli civakāma valli maṇāḷarē vārīr maṇimaṉṟa vāṇarē vārīr.
translation: Come, Bridegroom of Chidambara Valli, Sivakama Valli, come! O Lord of the Gem-Hall, come!
commentary: Vallalar uses tender, personal names for God drawn from familiar tradition. Chidambaram is a famous temple where the deity Siva is worshipped as the cosmic dancer, and Sivakama Valli is his divine consort. By calling God the "Bridegroom" and "Lord of the Gem-Hall," Vallalar expresses a deep, personal love for the ultimate reality, using the language and imagery he holds most dear.

sections.title: The Coming of the Dancer of the Hall to Embrace

translit: aṇaiyavā rīr eṉṉai aṇaiyavā rīr aṇivaḷarciṟ ṟampalattīr aṇaiyavā rīr.
translation: Come to embrace me, come to embrace me! O You of the beautifully flourishing Hall of Consciousness, come to embrace me.
commentary: This is the soul's passionate cry for union with the divine. The repetition shows an overwhelming longing. By addressing God as "You of the Hall of Consciousness (ciṟṟampalam)," Vallalar is calling to the divine presence that dwells both in the cosmos and within the sacred space of one's own awareness. The plea is for that inner presence to become a felt, loving embrace.

tamil: என்னுடைய நாயகரே அணையவா ரீர். அணையவா ரீர்
translit: iyaṟkaiuṇmai vaṭiviṉarē aṇaiyavā rīr ellāmcey vallavarē aṇaiyavā rīr iyaṟkaiviḷak kattavarē aṇaiyavā rīr ellārkkum nallavarē aṇaiyavā rīr iyaṟkaiiṉpa māṉavarē aṇaiyavā rīr iṟaimaiyelām uṭaiyavarē aṇaiyavā rīr iyaṟkainiṟai vāṉavarē aṇaiyavā rīr eṉṉuṭaiya nāyakarē aṇaiyavā rīr. aṇaiyavā rīr
translation: O You whose form is natural truth, come to embrace me. O You with the power to do everything, come to embrace me. O You who are the natural effulgence, come to embrace me. O You who are good to everyone, come to embrace me. O You who are natural bliss, come to embrace me. O You who possess all sovereignty, come to embrace me. O You who are natural plenitude, come to embrace me. O my Lord, come to embrace me. Come to embrace me.
commentary: The soul praises God by focusing on what is inherent to the divine nature. God's truth, light, and bliss are God's very essence, described by the repeated word iyarkai (natural). The plea is addressed to a being who is the fundamental source of reality, goodness, and joy.

tamil: என்னுடைய நாயகரே அணையவா ரீர். அணையவா ரீர்
translit: ulakamellām uṭaiyavarē aṇaiyavā rīr uṇmaiuraik kiṉṟavarē aṇaiyavā rīr kalakamaṟut tāṇṭavarē aṇaiyavā rīr kaṇṇaṉaiya kātalarē aṇaiyavā rīr alakaṟiyāp perumaiyarē aṇaiyavā rīr aṟputappoṟ cōtiyarē aṇaiyavā rīr ilakucapā patiyavarē aṇaiyavā rīr eṉṉuṭaiya nāyakarē aṇaiyavā rīr. aṇaiyavā rīr
translation: O You who possess all the worlds, come to embrace me. O You who speak the truth, come to embrace me. O You who ruled me, ending my turmoil, come to embrace me. O lover, precious as my own eyes, come to embrace me. O You of immeasurable greatness, come to embrace me. O wondrous golden Jothi, come to embrace me. O shining Lord of the Hall, come to embrace me. O my Lord, come to embrace me. Come to embrace me.
commentary: The relationship with God becomes deeply personal in this verse. God is the master of the cosmos and the one who brings peace to the soul's inner "turmoil." He is a lover more precious than one's own eyes, and the "wondrous golden Jothi," the Supreme Light that is central to Vallalar's path.

tamil: என்னுடைய நாயகரே அணையவா ரீர். அணையவா ரீர்
translit: potuvilnaṭik kiṉṟavarē aṇaiyavā rīr poṟpuṭaiya puṇṇiyarē aṇaiyavā rīr matuviliṉik kiṉṟavarē aṇaiyavā rīr maṉṉiyaeṉ maṉṉavarē aṇaiyavā rīr vituviṉamu tāṉavarē aṇaiyavā rīr meyyuraitta vittakarē aṇaiyavā rīr itutaruṇam iṟaiyavarē aṇaiyavā rīr eṉṉuṭaiya nāyakarē aṇaiyavā rīr. aṇaiyavā rīr
translation: O You who dance in the Common Hall, come to embrace me. O beautiful, virtuous One, come to embrace me. O You who are sweeter than honey, come to embrace me. O my eternal King, come to embrace me. O You who are the nectar of the moon, come to embrace me. O Master who spoke the truth, come to embrace me. O Lord, this is the moment, come to embrace me. O my Lord, come to embrace me. Come to embrace me.
commentary: The soul's yearning reaches its climax with the declaration, "this is the moment." The experience of God is described with images of overwhelming sweetness, like honey or the moon's nectar. By calling God the one who dances in the "Common Hall" (potu), Vallalar affirms that this divine bliss is available to all, and the time for his own union has finally arrived.

tamil: என்னுடைய நாயகரே அணையவா ரீர். அணையவா ரீர்
translit: viṉaimālai nīttavarē aṇaiyavā rīr vētamuṭip poruḷavarē aṇaiyavā rīr aṉaimālaik kāttavarē aṇaiyavā rīr aruṭperuñcō tippatiyīr aṇaiyavā rīr puṉaimālai vēyntavarē aṇaiyavā rīr potuvilniṟai pūraṇarē aṇaiyavā rīr eṉaimālai yiṭṭavarē aṇaiyavā rīr eṉṉuṭaiya nāyakarē aṇaiyavā rīr. aṇaiyavā rīr
translation: O You who removed the garland of my past deeds, come to embrace me. O You who are the substance at the crown of the Vedas, come to embrace me. O You who protected me from the garland of suffering, come to embrace me. O Lord of the Vast Grace-Light, come to embrace me. O You who wore the adorned garland, come to embrace me. O perfect plenitude who fills the Common Hall, come to embrace me. O You who placed a garland upon me, come to embrace me. O my Lord, come to embrace me. Come to embrace me.
commentary: This verse contrasts two kinds of 'garlands'. God removes the heavy garland of past deeds (karma) and suffering from the devotee. In its place, God offers a new garland, a symbol of divine acceptance and grace. The ultimate reality is revealed as a concept from the Vedas (ancient scriptures) and as the 'Lord of the Vast Grace-Light' (ArutPerunJothi), a living, saving presence.

tamil: என்னுடைய நாயகரே அணையவா ரீர். அணையவா ரீர்
translit: ciṟuvayatil eṉaiviḻaintīr aṇaiyavā rīr cittacikā maṇiyēnīr aṇaiyavā rīr uṟuvayatiṅ kitutaruṇam aṇaiyavā rīr uṇmaicoṉṉa uttamarē aṇaiyavā rīr poṟumaimika uṭaiyavarē aṇaiyavā rīr poyyāta vācakarē aṇaiyavā rīr iṟutitavirt tāṇṭavarē aṇaiyavā rīr eṉṉuṭaiya nāyakarē aṇaiyavā rīr. aṇaiyavā rīr
translation: You desired me in my youth, come embrace me. O crest-jewel of the Siddhas, come embrace me. This is the prime of my age, this is the moment, come embrace me. O perfect one who spoke the truth, come embrace me. O you who are so very patient, come embrace me. O you of unfailing words, come embrace me. O you who averted my final end and took me as your own, come embrace me. O my Lord, come embrace me. Come embrace me.
commentary: The relationship with God is described as a lifelong love story, one that began when God desired the devotee in his youth. Now, at the 'prime of his age,' the devotee feels the time for union is ripe. God is praised as the ultimate among the Siddhas (perfected spiritual masters) and as a patient, truthful guide who has saved him from death itself.

tamil: என்னுடைய நாயகரே அணையவா ரீர். அணையவா ரீர்
translit: cātimatan tavirttavarē aṇaiyavā rīr taṉittalaimaip perumpatiyīr aṇaiyavā rīr ātiyantam illavarē aṇaiyavā rīr āraṇaṅkaḷ pōṟṟaniṉṟīr aṇaiyavā rīr ōtiyuṇar variyavarē aṇaiyavā rīr uḷḷapaṭi uraittavarē aṇaiyavā rīr īticainta taruṇamiṅkē aṇaiyavā rīr eṉṉuṭaiya nāyakarē aṇaiyavā rīr. aṇaiyavā rīr
translation: O you who abolished caste and religion, come embrace me. O great sovereign of singular supremacy, come embrace me. O you who have no beginning or end, come embrace me. You stand praised by the Vedas, come embrace me. O you who are difficult to grasp through study, come embrace me. O you who spoke the truth just as it is, come embrace me. This here is the fitting moment, come embrace me. O my Lord, come embrace me. Come embrace me.
commentary: A core teaching appears here: God is the one who has abolished caste and religion. This truth is praised by the Vedas, yet it cannot be grasped by study alone; it must be known directly. Vallalar presents a God who is universal, without beginning or end, who spoke the truth just as it is, and who is open to all.

tamil: என்னுடைய நாயகரே அணையவா ரீர். அணையவா ரீர்
translit: aṉpāṭṭai viḻaintavarē aṇaiyavā rīr aruṭcōti vaṭiviṉarē aṇaiyavā rīr tuṉpāṭṭai oḻittavarē aṇaiyavā rīr turiyaniṟai periyavarē aṇaiyavā rīr piṉpāṭṭuk kālaiyitē aṇaiyavā rīr piccēṟṟu kiṉṟavarē aṇaiyavā rīr eṉpāṭṭai ēṟṟavarē aṇaiyavā rīr eṉṉuṭaiya nāyakarē aṇaiyavā rīr. aṇaiyavā rīr
translation: O you who desire the play of love, come embrace me. O you in the form of Grace-Light, come embrace me. O you who ended the play of suffering, come embrace me. O great one full of Turiyam, come embrace me. This is the time for the final act, come embrace me. O you who are driving me mad with love, come embrace me. O you who accepted my song, come embrace me. O my Lord, come embrace me. Come embrace me.
commentary: The culmination of this longing is an ecstatic madness, a 'play of love' that ends all suffering. The devotee feels God is actively driving him mad with love and has accepted his songs of devotion. This state of union is called Turiyam, a boundless awareness beyond the ordinary states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.

tamil: என்னுடைய நாயகரே அணையவா ரீர். அணையவா ரீர்
translit: araikkaṇamum tariyēṉnāṉ aṇaiyavā rīr āṇaiummēl āṇaieṉṉai aṇaiyavā rīr puraikkaṇaṅkaṇ ṭaṟiyēṉnāṉ aṇaiyavā rīr poṉmēṉip puṇṇiyarē aṇaiyavā rīr varaikkaṇañcey vittavarē aṇaiyavā rīr maṉṟilnaṭik kiṉṟavarē aṇaiyavā rīr iraikkaṇavu taruṇamitē aṇaiyavā rīr eṉṉuṭaiya nāyakarē aṇaiyavā rīr. aṇaiyavā rīr
translation: I cannot bear this for even half a second, come embrace me. I swear upon you, I swear it, come and embrace me. I have never seen a single fault in you, come embrace me. O holy one with a golden body, come embrace me. O you who made the mountain bow, come embrace me. O you who dance in the sacred Hall, come embrace me. This is the perfect moment for our union, come embrace me. O my Lord, come embrace me. Come embrace me.
commentary: The speaker's longing has become so acute that waiting even a moment longer is unbearable. Invoking classic images of Lord Siva, the cosmic dancer and the all-powerful being with a radiant golden body, the soul swears an oath, declaring that this very instant is the perfect time for their embrace.

tamil: என்னுடைய நாயகரே அணையவா ரீர். அணையவா ரீர்
translit: karuṇainaṭañ ceypavarē aṇaiyavā rīr kaṇmaṇiyil kalantavarē aṇaiyavā rīr aruḷniṟaiciṟ capaiyavarē aṇaiyavā rīr aṉparkuṟai tīrttavarē aṇaiyavā rīr taruṇamitu virainteṉṉai aṇaiyavā rīr cattiyarē nittiyarē aṇaiyavā rīr iruḷniṟaintārk kaṟivariyīr aṇaiyavā rīr eṉṉuṭaiya nāyakarē aṇaiyavā rīr. aṇaiyavā rīr
translation: O you who perform the dance of compassion, come embrace me. O you who have mingled in the pupil of my eye, come embrace me. O you of the grace-filled Chit Sabhai, come embrace me. O you who resolve the woes of your devotees, come embrace me. This is the moment; come quickly and embrace me. O one who is Truth, O one who is Eternal, come embrace me. You are impossible to know for those filled with darkness, come embrace me. O my Lord, come embrace me. Come embrace me.
commentary: The true nature of God is compassion, expressed as a continuous dance. This presence is intimately felt "in the pupil of my eye," residing within the devotee's own heart, the true Hall of Consciousness (Chit Sabhai). Only those clouded by their own inner darkness fail to see this ever-present, eternal Truth.

tamil: என்னுடைய நாயகரே அணையவா ரீர். அணையவா ரீர்
translit: cēra:ummēl ācaikoṇṭēṉ aṇaiyavā rīr tiruvuḷamē aṟintatellām aṇaiyavā rīr āreṉakkiṅ kummaiyallāl aṇaiyavā rīr ayalaṟiyēṉ āṇaiummēl aṇaiyavā rīr īrakattēṉ alla:iṅkē aṇaiyavā rīr eṉṉācai poṅkukiṉṟa taṇaiyavā rīr ērakattē amarntaruḷvīr aṇaiyavā rīr eṉṉuṭaiya nāyakarē aṇaiyavā rīr. aṇaiyavā rīr
translation: I have conceived a desire to unite with you, please come embrace me. Your divine mind knows everything, please come embrace me. Who do I have here but you? Please come embrace me. I know no other, I swear upon you, please come embrace me. I am not of a divided heart here, please come embrace me. My desire is overflowing, please come embrace me. You who graciously reside in Erakam (a sacred abode of Lord Murugan), please come embrace me. My Lord, please come embrace me, please come embrace me.
commentary: The soul's devotion is absolute and undivided. There is no other person, no other object of desire, and no other refuge but the Lord. Swearing an oath to this singular focus, the speaker declares that their heart is whole, overflowing with a single, powerful longing for union.

translit: kalantukoḷa vēṇṭukiṉṟēṉ aṇaiyavā rīr kātalpoṅku kiṉṟateṉṉai aṇaiyavā rīr pulantaṟiyēṉ viraikiṉṟēṉ aṇaiyavā rīr puṇarvataṟkut taruṇamitē aṇaiyavā rīr alantaviṭat taruḷkiṉṟīr aṇaiyavā rīr araikkaṇamum iṉittariyēṉ aṇaiyavā rīr ilantainaṟuṅ kaṉiyaṉaiyīraṇaiyavā rīr eṉṉuṭaiya nāyakarē aṇaiyavā rīr.
translation: I beg to merge with you, please come embrace me. Love is overflowing within me, please come embrace me. I do not feign lover's quarrels; I am rushing to you, please come embrace me. This is the moment for our union, please come embrace me. You grant grace in times of distress, please come embrace me. I cannot bear this for even half a moment longer, please come embrace me. You who are like a sweet, fragrant jujube fruit, please come embrace me. My Lord, please come embrace me.
commentary: This is a final, breathless plea for union, driven by an overflowing love. The speaker abandons all pretense and rushes toward God, declaring that waiting any longer is impossible. Comparing the Lord to a "sweet, fragrant jujube fruit" transforms the awesome divine into something irresistibly, intimately desirable.

translit: aṇaiyavā rīreṉṉai aṇaiyavā rīr aṇivaḷarciṟ ṟampalattīr aṇaiyavā rīr.
translation: Please come embrace me, oh, come embrace me. You who are in the ever-beautifying Chitrambalam, please come embrace me.
commentary: This final, concentrated plea identifies the divine beloved with the dweller in Chitrambalam, the sacred hall of pure consciousness. The embrace the soul seeks is with a personal deity and with the ultimate reality at the very heart of existence.
NOTES

translit: aṇikiḷar - mutaṟpatippu., po. cu., pi. irā., ca. mu. ka.
translation: aṇikiḷar — reading of the first edition, of Po. Su., of P. Irā., and of S. Mu. Ka.

sections.title: The Dancer of the Hall Comes to Dance

translit: āṭavā rīr eṉṉō ṭāṭavā rīr ampalattil āṭukiṉṟīr āṭavā rīr.
translation: Come dance, come dance with me. You who dance in the Ampalam, come dance.
commentary: The relationship with God has shifted from a one-sided plea for an embrace to a mutual invitation to dance. The soul is no longer a passive supplicant but an active partner, ready to join in the joyful, cosmic play of the divine within the Ampalam, the inner hall of consciousness.

tamil: என்னுடைய நாயகரே ஆடவா ரீர் ஆடவா ரீர்
translit: taṉmaipiṟark kaṟivariyīr āṭavā rīr taṉittalaimaip perumpatiyīr āṭavā rīr vaṉmaimaṉat tavarkkariyīr āṭavā rīr vañcamilā neñcakattīr āṭavā rīr toṉmaimaṟai muṭiyamarntīr āṭavā rīr turiyapataṅ kaṭantavarē āṭavā rīr iṉmaitavirt teṉaimaṇantīr āṭavā rīr. eṉṉuṭaiya nāyakarē āṭavā rīr āṭavā rīr
translation: You whose nature is difficult for others to know, come dance. You who are the great Lord of singular supremacy, come dance. You who are unattainable to the hard-hearted, come dance. You who dwell in guileless hearts, come dance. You who are seated on the crown of the ancient scriptures, come dance. You who have transcended the state of turiyam, come dance. You who dispelled my poverty and married me, come dance. My Lord, come dance, come dance.
commentary: The soul lists God's qualities to call him forth: he is both supreme and unknowable, yet lives inside the innocent heart. Vallalar notes that God is beyond even the highest spiritual states like turiyam (the fourth state of consciousness beyond waking, dreaming, and deep sleep). By stating "you... married me," the speaker affirms that the union is already a reality, and this dance is a celebration of that established bond.

tamil: என்னுடைய நாயகரே ஆடவா ரீர். ஆடவா ரீர்
translit: tiruvāḷar pōṟṟa eṉṉō ṭāṭavā rīr tiruvaṉaiyār vāḻtta:iṅkē āṭavā rīr peruvāymaip peruntakaiyīr āṭavā rīr pērācai poṅkukiṉṟēṉ āṭavā rīr uruvāki ōṅkukiṉṟīr āṭavā rīr uttamarē itutaruṇam āṭavā rīr iruvāṇar ēttaniṉṟīr āṭavā rīr eṉṉuṭaiya nāyakarē āṭavā rīr. āṭavā rīr
translation: As the prosperous praise you, come dance with me. As women like the goddess Thiru bless you, come dance here. You who are the great being of great truth, come dance. I am overflowing with immense desire, come dance. You take form and rise high, come dance. O perfect one, this is the moment, come dance. You who stand praised by the two kinds of celestials, come dance. My Lord, come dance. Come dance.
commentary: The intimate dance between the soul and God becomes a public, cosmic event, celebrated by all. The plea "this is the moment" returns, emphasizing that divine union is both an eternal truth and an experience that happens in a specific, perfect instant.

tamil: என்னுடைய நாயகரே ஆடவா ரீர். ஆடவா ரீர்
translit: vēṟṟumukam pārēṉeṉṉō ṭāṭavā rīr veṭkamellām viṭṭuviṭṭēṉ āṭavā rīr māṟṟutaṟkeṇ ṇātireṉṉō ṭāṭavā rīr māṟṟiluyir māyppēṉkaṇṭīr āṭavā rīr kūṟṟutaitta cēvaṭiyīr āṭavā rīr koṇṭukulaṅ kuṟiyātīr āṭavā rīr ēṟṟataṉit taruṇamītē āṭavā rīr eṉṉuṭaiya nāyakarē āṭavā rīr. āṭavā rīr
translation: I will not look at another face, come dance with me. I have abandoned all shame, come dance. Do not think of changing this, come dance with me. If you change, I will surely end my life, come dance. You with the sacred red feet that kicked Death, come dance. You who do not consider caste when you accept someone, come dance. This is the fitting, singular moment, come dance. My Lord, come dance. Come dance.
commentary: Here, the soul declares her absolute, life-or-death devotion. By abandoning shame, she casts off all worldly conventions for the sake of her divine love. This verse also contains a key social teaching: God accepts all people without considering their caste or social status. Her love is for the one who has conquered Death itself, and she will accept no other.

tamil: என்னுடைய நாயகரே ஆடவா ரீர். ஆடவா ரீர்
translit: illāmai nīkkiniṉṟīr āṭavā rīr eṉṉaimaṇa mālaiyiṭṭīr āṭavā rīr kollāmai neṟieṉṟīr āṭavā rīr kuṟṟamelāṅ kuṇaṅkoṇṭīr āṭavā rīr nallārcol nallavarē āṭavā rīr naṟṟāyil iṉiyavarē āṭavā rīr ellāmcey vallavarē āṭavā rīr eṉṉuṭaiya nāyakarē āṭavā rīr. āṭavā rīr
translation: You stood having removed my destitution, come dance. You placed the wedding garland on me, come dance. You declared the path of non-killing, come dance. You took all my faults as virtues, come dance. O good one, acclaimed by the good, come dance. You who are sweeter than a good mother, come dance. You who are the potent one, capable of doing everything, come dance. My Lord, come dance. Come dance.
commentary: The soul's plea is grounded in gratitude for all that God has already done. He is the one who has personally transformed her life. He has provided for her, taught her the supreme virtue of non-killing (kollāmai), accepted her flaws, and shown a tenderness greater than a mother's. This history of grace gives her the confidence to ask for the final union of the dance.

tamil: என்னுடைய நாயகரே ஆடவா ரீர். ஆடவா ரீர்
translit: ācaikoṇṭēṉ āṭaeṉṉō ṭāṭavā rīr ācaiveṭkam aṟiyātāl āṭavā rīr ōcaikoṇṭa teṅkumiṅkē āṭavā rīr umāṇai ummaiviṭēṉ āṭavā rīr kācupaṇat tācaiyilēṉ āṭavā rīr kaipiṭittāṟ pōtumeṉṉō ṭāṭavā rīr ēcaṟalnīt teṉaiāṇṭīr āṭavā rīr eṉṉuṭaiya nāyakarē āṭavā rīr. āṭavā rīr
translation: I am filled with desire; come dance with me, come dance. My desire knows no shame, so come dance, come dance. Sound has filled this whole place; come dance, come dance. I swear on you, I will not let you go; come dance, come dance. I have no desire for cash or money; come dance, come dance. It is enough if you take my hand; come dance with me, come dance. You ruled me, removing all my sorrow; come dance, come dance. My Lord, come dance, come dance. Come dance, come dance.
commentary: The desire that drives the soul is not for worldly things but for God alone. She makes it clear that she has no want for money or status; the simple touch of God's hand is enough. Her love is so consuming that it knows no shame or restraint, and having felt his presence, she playfully vows never to let him go.

tamil: என்னுடைய நாயகரே ஆடவா ரீர். ஆடவா ரீர்
translit: caṉmārkka neṟivaittīr āṭavā rīr cākāta varantantīr āṭavā rīr kaṉmārkka maṉaṅkaraittīr āṭavā rīr kaṇṇicainta kaṇavarēnīr āṭavā rīr coṉmārkkap poruḷāṉīr āṭavā rīr cuttaaruṭ cōtiyarē āṭavā rīr eṉmārkkam uḷattukantīr āṭavā rīr eṉṉuṭaiya nāyakarē āṭavā rīr. āṭavā rīr
translation: You established the path of Sanmarkkam; come dance, come dance. You gave the boon of deathlessness; come dance, come dance. You melted my stone-hard heart; come dance, come dance. You are the husband my eyes approved; come dance, come dance. You became the meaning of the path of scripture; come dance, come dance. O pure Grace-Jothi! Come dance, come dance. You delighted in my path within your heart; come dance, come dance. My Lord, come dance, come dance. Come dance, come dance.
commentary: This verse connects the soul's personal love story to Vallalar's universal teachings. The intimate union she seeks is the fruit of following Sanmarkkam (the true path of harmony and compassion). This path, established by God, leads to the boon of a deathless life and a melting of the hard heart. Her "husband" is revealed to be the pure Grace-Jothi, the divine Light itself.

tamil: என்னுடைய நாயகரே ஆடவா ரீர். ஆடவா ரீர்
translit: aṇṭamelām kaṇṭavarē āṭavā rīr akaṇṭapari pūraṇarē āṭavā rīr paṇṭamelām paṭaittavarē āṭavā rīr paṟṟoṭuvī ṭillavarē āṭavā rīr koṇṭeṉaivan tāṇṭavarē āṭavā rīr kūttāṭa vallavarē āṭavā rīr eṇtakupoṟ capaiyuṭaiyīr āṭavā rīr eṉṉuṭaiya nāyakarē āṭavā rīr. āṭavā rīr
translation: O one who has seen all universes! Come dance, come dance. O indivisible, perfect fullness! Come dance, come dance. O creator of all things! Come dance, come dance. O one who has neither attachment nor liberation! Come dance, come dance. O one who came and took me to rule me! Come dance, come dance. O one skilled in dancing the cosmic dance! Come dance, come dance. You who possess the esteemed Golden Hall! Come dance, come dance. My Lord, come dance, come dance. Come dance, come dance.
commentary: The soul calls out to God by naming His vast, cosmic qualities: creator of universes, indivisible fullness, the great cosmic dancer. These grand descriptions are paired with a deeply personal one, for this same universal Being came specifically to claim and rule the individual soul. The reference to one who has "neither attachment nor liberation" points to a state beyond all dualities, a supreme freedom.

tamil: என்னுடைய நாயகரே ஆடவா ரீர். ஆடவா ரீர்
translit: pētaniṉai yātuvirain tāṭavā rīr piṉpāṭṭuk kālaiyitē āṭavā rīr ōta:ula vātavarē āṭavā rīr uḷḷācai poṅkukiṉṟa tāṭavā rīr cātalaṟut teṉaiāṇṭīr āṭavā rīr taṉittalaimaip perumpatiyīr āṭavā rīr ētamaṟut tavarkkiṉiyīr āṭavā rīr eṉṉuṭaiya nāyakarē āṭavā rīr. āṭavā rīr
translation: Without thinking of differences, hurry and come dance, come dance. This is the time for what follows; come dance, come dance. O One whose praise never runs out, however much it is sung! Come dance, come dance. My inner desire is surging; come dance, come dance. You ruled me, cutting off death; come dance, come dance. O great Lord of unique supremacy! Come dance, come dance. O one who is sweet to those whose faults you have removed! Come dance, come dance. My Lord, come dance, come dance. Come dance, come dance.
commentary: A sense of urgency fills this verse. The soul pleads with God to come quickly, setting aside all distinctions, because the desire for union is overwhelming now. God is the One whose praise never runs out, who cut off death and ruled the soul, and who is sweet to those whose faults He has removed.

tamil: என்னுடைய நாயகரே ஆடவா ரீர். ஆடவா ரீர்
translit: kaḷḷamoṉṟum aṟiyēṉnāṉ āṭavā rīr kaikalantu koṇṭīreṉṉō ṭāṭavā rīr uḷḷapaṭi uraikkiṉṟēṉ āṭavā rīr ummācai poṅkukiṉṟa tāṭavā rīr taḷḷariyēṉ eṉṉōṭiṅkē āṭavā rīr tāḻkkiliṟai yumtariyēṉ āṭavā rīr eḷḷalaṟut tāṇṭukoṇṭīr āṭavā rīr eṉṉuṭaiya nāyakarē āṭavā rīr. āṭavā rīr
