Vallalar identifies this victorious God as Ampalavāṇan, the Lord who dances in the cosmic hall of consciousness, a central image for God in the Tamil tradition.

translit: eṉuyir kāttāṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē iṉpam palittateṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē poṉurut tantāṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē poṟcapai appaṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē.
translation: Blow the conch, for he protected my soul. Blow the conch, for bliss has come to fruition. Blow the conch, for he gave me a golden form. Blow the conch, for he is the Father of the Golden Hall.
commentary: God's protection culminates in a physical transformation into a "golden form" and the realization of lasting bliss. This golden body is a key teaching, signifying the perfection of the physical self into an immortal vessel of light. This transformation occurs in the Poṟsabai, the Golden Hall of consciousness, where God dwells as a loving Father.

translit: civamākkikkoṇṭāṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē ciṟṟam palattāṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē navanōk kaḷittāṉ eṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē nāṉavaṉ āṉēṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē.
translation: He made me into Sivam, blow, O conch, blow! He is the one of the Chitrambalam, blow, O conch, blow! He bestowed the ninefold gaze, blow, O conch, blow! I have become He, blow, O conch, blow!
commentary: This verse proclaims the highest spiritual attainment: union with God. To be "made into Sivam" means the soul has merged with the divine, losing its separate identity. The declaration "I have become He" is the ultimate expression of this non-dual experience, realized in the Chitrambalam, the inner hall of pure consciousness.

translit: nāta muṭiyāṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē ñāṉacapaiyāṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē pāta maḷittāṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē palittatu pūcaieṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē.
translation: He wears Naatham as his crown, blow, O conch, blow! He is the one of the Gnanasabai, blow, O conch, blow! He granted his feet, blow, O conch, blow! The worship has borne fruit, blow, O conch, blow!
commentary: God's nature is proclaimed as Naatham, the primal cosmic sound, which He wears as a crown. He presides in the Gnanasabai, the inner hall of pure wisdom. To be "granted his feet" is a traditional way of saying one has received divine grace and found ultimate refuge, a sign that the long path of worship has reached its goal.

translit: teḷḷamu tāṉāṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē ciṟcapai appaṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē uḷḷam uvantāṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē uḷḷa turaittāṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē.
translation: He became the clear nectar, blow, O conch, blow! He is the Father in the Cirsabai, blow, O conch, blow! He rejoiced in His heart, blow, O conch, blow! He spoke what is real, blow, O conch, blow!
commentary: The conch announces that God is experienced as a "clear nectar" of pure bliss. This experience takes place in the Cirsabai (hall of consciousness), where God is felt as a loving Father. Beautifully, Vallalar notes that God himself "rejoiced," showing that the divine partakes in the joy of this union and reveals ultimate truth directly.

translit: eṉṉaṟi vāṉāṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē ellāmcey vallāṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē cennilai tantāṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē ciṟcapai appaṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē.
translation: He became my own knowing, blow, O conch, blow! He is the one who can do everything, blow, O conch, blow! He granted the perfect state, blow, O conch, blow! He is the Father in the Cirsabai, blow, O conch, blow!
commentary: Here, the union with God is described as the dissolution of all otherness: God becomes the devotee's own knowing. This is the "perfect state," a gift from the omnipotent Father who resides in the Cirsabai. In this state, the distinction between the self and the divine, between the knower and what is known, has vanished.

translit: iṟavāmai īntāṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē eṇṇam palittateṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē tiṟamē aḷittāṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē ciṟṟam palattāṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē.
translation: He bestowed deathlessness, blow, O conch, blow! My intention has been fulfilled, blow, O conch, blow! He bestowed true power, blow, O conch, blow! He is the one of the Chitrambalam, blow, O conch, blow!
commentary: The conch announces the greatest spiritual attainment: the gift of a deathless existence. The soul's deepest longing is fulfilled by the divine, who is the reality of the Chitrambalam, the sacred expanse of consciousness. This is a promise and a realized state.

translit: karavu tavirntateṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē karuṇai kiṭaittateṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē iravu viṭintateṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē eṇṇam palittateṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē.
translation: Blow the conch, for deceit is gone. Blow the conch, for grace is received. Blow the conch, for the night has dawned. Blow the conch, for my wish is fulfilled.
commentary: This verse declares the end of the soul's long struggle. The "night" of ignorance and illusion is over, and the "day" of divine grace has begun. All falsehood has vanished, and the soul's ultimate purpose has been achieved.

translit: ellāmcey vallāṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē ellārkkum nallāṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē ellām uṭaiyāṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē ellāmum āṉāṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē.
translation: Blow the conch, for He has the power to do everything. Blow the conch, for He is good to everyone. Blow the conch, for He possesses everything. Blow the conch, for He has become everything.
commentary: The conch proclaims the absolute nature of God. The divine is simultaneously all-powerful, all-good, the source of all things, and the very substance of everything that exists. There is nothing outside of this universal, benevolent reality.

translit: karuṇā nitiyareṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē kaṭavuḷ avaṉēeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē aruḷnā ṭakattāṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē ampalac cōtieṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē.
translation: Blow the conch, for He is a treasury of compassion. Blow the conch, for He alone is God. Blow the conch, for He performs the sacred drama of grace. Blow the conch, for He is the Jothi of the Ambalam.
commentary: God's defining quality is compassion, a boundless treasury. The universe and our lives are a divine play of grace, and God's true form is Jothi, a vast effulgence of light experienced in the Ambalam, the sacred expanse of consciousness.

translit: taṉṉikar illāṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē talaivaṉ avaṉēeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē poṉṉiyal vaṇṇaṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē potunaṭam ceyvāṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē.
translation: Blow the conch, for He is without equal. Blow the conch, for He alone is the Master. Blow the conch, for His complexion is like gold. Blow the conch, for He performs the cosmic dance.
commentary: God's uniqueness and supreme mastery are proclaimed here. The description of a golden complexion connects God with light, purity, and preciousness, while the cosmic dance refers to the constant, dynamic activity of the universe, which is God's own performance.

translit: āṉanta nātaṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē aruḷuṭai appaṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē tāṉantam illāṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē tattuvac cōtieṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē.
translation: Blow the conch, for He is the Lord of Bliss. Blow the conch, for He is the gracious Father. Blow the conch, for He Himself is eternal. Blow the conch, for He is the Jothi of Reality.
commentary: Here, God is described in both personal and ultimate terms. He is the intimate, gracious Father and the Lord of Bliss, but also the eternal, uncaused Reality and its illuminating essence, the Jothi of Truth itself.

translit: poyviṭ ṭakaṉṟēṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē puṇṇiyaṉ āṉēṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē meytoṭṭu niṉṟēṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē mēlveḷi kaṇṭēṉeṉṟu ūtūtu caṅkē.
translation: Blow the conch, proclaiming I have abandoned falsehood. Blow the conch, proclaiming I have become a virtuous one. Blow the conch, proclaiming I have grasped the Truth and stand firm. Blow the conch, proclaiming I have seen the Supreme Space.
commentary: The focus suddenly shifts from praising God to the devotee's own transformation. The real fruit of devotion is nearness to God and a fundamental change in oneself: falsehood is gone, truth is realized, and the highest spiritual state, the Supreme Space, is directly experienced. The conch now announces a personal victory.

translit: ampalavar vantāreṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi aṟputamcey kiṉṟāreṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi cempalaṉ aḷittāreṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi cittinilai peṟṟateṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi.
translation: The Lord of the Ambalam has come, sound the trumpet! He is performing miracles, sound the trumpet! He has granted the ultimate good, sound the trumpet! The state of siddhi has been achieved, sound the trumpet!
commentary: The great announcement is that God has arrived within the devotee's own being. This inner space is called the Ambalam (the sacred hall of consciousness). This arrival grants siddhi, or supernatural abilities, signifying a complete transformation of the self.

translit: ciṟcapaiyaik kaṇṭōmeṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi cittikaḷcey kiṉṟōmeṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi poṟcapai pukuntōmeṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi puntimakiḻ kiṉṟōmeṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi.
translation: We have seen the Chit Sabhai, sound the trumpet! We are performing siddhis, sound the trumpet! We have entered the Por Sabhai, sound the trumpet! Our minds are rejoicing, sound the trumpet!
commentary: The devotee proclaims what has happened: we have seen the Chit Sabhai (Hall of Consciousness), we have entered the Por Sabhai (Golden Hall), and we are performing siddhis. These are accomplished facts, and the mind rejoices in them.

translit: ñāṉacittipurameṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi nāṭakamcey iṭameṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi āṉacitti ceyvōmeṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi aruṭcōti peṟṟōmeṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi.
translation: This is Gnana Siddhi Puram, sound the trumpet! This is the place where the divine play is performed, sound the trumpet! We will perform the resulting siddhis, sound the trumpet! We have received the Grace-Light, sound the trumpet!
commentary: Gnana Siddhi Puram, 'the city of wisdom and attainment', is the name Vallalar gave to Vadalur, where he raised the Sathya Gnana Sabai. He proclaims it the place where God's play of grace is performed, where the siddhis will be done, for the Arut Jothi, the Grace-Light, has been received.

translit: koṭikaṭṭikkoṇṭōmeṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi kūttāṭu kiṉṟōmeṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi aṭimuṭiyaik kaṇṭōmeṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi aruḷamutam uṇṭōmeṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi.
translation: We have hoisted our flag, sound the trumpet! We are dancing the divine dance, sound the trumpet! We have seen the feet and the crown, sound the trumpet! We have drunk the nectar of grace, sound the trumpet!
commentary: This verse uses powerful symbols of victory and celebration. Hoisting a flag declares the new reign of grace. The ecstatic dance is an expression of boundless joy. To have "seen the feet and the crown" means to have understood God in his entirety, from his most accessible aspect to his most transcendent mystery.

translit: apparvaru kiṉṟāreṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi aṟputamcey vataṟkeṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi ceppanilai peṟṟateṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi cittipuramiṭameṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi.
translation: Appar is coming, sound the trumpet! He comes to perform miracles, sound the trumpet! The state of perfection has been achieved, sound the trumpet! This place is Siddhi Puram, sound the trumpet!
commentary: The arrival of Appar (the Father, a name for God showing deep intimacy) is the final confirmation that this state of perfection has been reached. This place, Siddhi Puram (the city of attainment), is where the divine presence makes miracles an everyday reality.

translit: tāṉēnāṉ āṉēṉeṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi cattiyamcat tiyameṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi ūṉē pukuntateṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi oḷivaṇṇam āṉateṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi.
translation: Proclaim that I have become That itself. Proclaim that this is the truth, the truth. Proclaim that it has entered my very flesh. Proclaim that my body has taken on the color of light.
commentary: The experience deepens from seeing God to becoming one with God. This union is more than a mental state; it is a physical event that permeates the very flesh, causing the body itself to become luminous. Vallalar insists this is a literal truth, a physical transformation into a body of light.

translit: vēkātakāluṇarntu ciṉṉam piṭi vēkāta naṭutterintu ciṉṉam piṭi cākātatalaiaṟintu ciṉṉam piṭi cākāta kalvikaṟṟuc ciṉṉam piṭi.
translation: Proclaim that you have realized the un-burning breath. Proclaim that you have perceived the un-burning center. Proclaim that you have known the deathless principle. Proclaim that you have learned the art of immortality.
commentary: This verse points to the science of deathlessness (sākāk kalvi), the learning that does not die. Vallalar names its secrets: the breath that does not burn away (vēkāk kāl), the center that does not burn, the head that does not die (sākāt talai). He means deathlessness of the body itself, not the survival of the soul after death. This is not a philosophy to be learned from books, but a state to be embodied.

translit: mītāṉa nilaiēṟic ciṉṉam piṭi veṭṭaveḷi naṭuniṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi vētāka mamkaṭantu ciṉṉam piṭi vētāntac cittānta ciṉṉam piṭi.
translation: Proclaim that you have ascended to the highest state. Proclaim that you stand in the center of the vast, open expanse. Proclaim that you have transcended the Vedas and Agamas. Proclaim the culmination of Vedanta and Siddhanta.
commentary: The highest state is a direct experience of the ultimate reality, described here as standing in the center of the veṭṭaveḷi (the vast, open expanse). This experience transcends the knowledge contained in the Vedas and Agamas (Hinduism's sacred scriptures), representing the fulfillment and final goal of India's great philosophical traditions, Vedanta and Siddhanta.

translit: paṉmārkka mumkaṭantu ciṉṉam piṭi paṉṉiraṇṭiṉ mītuniṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi caṉmārkkam mārkkameṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi cattiyamcey kiṉṟōmeṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi.
translation: Proclaim that you have transcended all the many paths. Proclaim that you stand above the twelfth plane. Proclaim that Sanmarkkam is the one true path. Proclaim that we declare this on oath.
commentary: Having transcended all previous spiritual paths, one arrives at the ultimate truth of Sanmarkkam (the True Path). This path is realized by ascending to the "twelfth plane," a spiritual center beyond the commonly known chakras. Vallalar's declaration is more than a philosophical proposal; he presents it as a sworn testimony, a definitive and final truth for all.

translit: cittāṭu kiṉṟāreṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi cettār eḻuvāreṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi ittā raṇiyileṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi ituvē taruṇameṉṟu ciṉṉam piṭi.
translation: Proclaim that He is performing His divine games. Proclaim that the dead will rise. Proclaim that it will happen right here on this earth. Proclaim that now is the very moment.
commentary: A great miracle is about to unfold on Earth. Vallalar announces that God's "divine games" will include the literal resurrection of the dead. He stresses that this is not a symbolic event or one set in a distant heaven, but a physical reality that will happen on this Earth, imminently. The verse carries a powerful sense of urgency: the time is now.

translit: kaiyaṟavi lātunaṭuk kaṇpuruvap pūṭṭu kaṇṭukaḷi koṇṭutiṟan tuṇṭunaṭu nāṭṭu aiyarmika uyyumvakai apparviḷai yāṭṭu āṭuvateṉ ṟēmaṟaikaḷ pāṭuvatu pāṭṭu.
translation: Without despair, I found and joyfully opened the lock between the eyebrows, partaking of the essence in the central land. The Vedas sing that this is the Father's divine play, the way the Master ensures our great salvation.
commentary: The path to enlightenment is an inner path culminating in the opening of the "lock between the eyebrows," the spiritual center of inner vision. This breakthrough allows one to experience the divine essence directly. Vallalar frames this mystical event as a joyful "divine play" arranged by God to grant salvation.

translit: ciṟcapaiyum poṟcapaiyum contameṉa tāccu tēvarkaḷum mūvarkaḷum pēcuvateṉ pēccu iṟcamaya vāḻvileṉak keṉṉaiiṉi ēccu eṉpiṟapput tuṉpamelām iṉṟōṭē pōccu.
translation: The Hall of Consciousness and the Golden Hall have become my own. What the devas and the Trinity speak is my speech. In this life of worldly religion, what reproach can there be for me now? All the suffering of my birth has ended as of today.
commentary: The Hall of Consciousness (cit-sabai) and the Golden Hall have become Vallalar's own. Even the devas and the Three now speak his words. Living in a world of religions, no reproach can touch him any longer, for all the suffering of birth has ended today.

translit: aiyararuṭ cōtiyara cāṭcieṉa tāccu āraṇamum ākamamum pēcuvateṉ pēccu eyyulaka vāḻvileṉak keṉṉaiiṉi ēccu eṉpiṟavit tuṉpamelām iṉṟōṭē pōccu.
translation: The reign of the Master's Grace-Jothi has become my own. What the Vedas and the Agamas speak is my speech. In this wearying worldly life, what reproach can there be for me now? All the suffering of my birth has ended as of today.
commentary: Having realized God, the speaker now embodies the authority of Grace and scripture. The reign of ArutJothi (Grace-Light) has become his own inner reality. His words now channel the essential truth of the Vedas and Agamas (sacred texts), from direct experience of their source. This inner realization makes worldly criticism and suffering irrelevant.

translit: īcaṉaru ḷālkaṭalil ēṟṟatoru ōṭam ēṟikkarai ēṟiṉēṉ iruntatoru māṭam tēcuṟumam māṭanaṭut teyvamaṇi pīṭam tīpaoḷi kaṇṭavuṭaṉ cērntatucan tōṭam.
translation: By the Lord's grace, I boarded a boat on the ocean, climbed out, and reached the shore. There stood a mansion. In the center of that radiant mansion was a divine, jeweled throne. Upon seeing the light of the lamp, I was filled with joy.
commentary: This verse presents the spiritual quest as a voyage. The turbulent "ocean" is worldly life, and the "boat" is God's grace, which carries the soul to the "shore" of spiritual stability. The "mansion" represents the realized state of consciousness, and at its very heart is a "lamp," the divine Light of the Self, the sight of which brings great joy.

translit: mērumalai ucciyilvi ḷaṅkukampa nīṭci mēvumataṉ mēlulakil vīṟumara cāṭci cērumatil kaṇṭapala kāṭcikaḷkaṇ kāṭci ceppalari tāmitaṟkeṉ appaṉaruḷ cāṭci.
translation: On the peak of Mount Meru, a shining pillar extends. Above it, in the world beyond, is a magnificent reign. The many visions I saw there are a true spectacle for the eyes. It is difficult to describe them; my Father's grace is the witness to this.
commentary: The highest spiritual visions defy description. Mount Meru, the mythical center of the cosmos, also symbolizes the human spine, with its peak at the crown of the head. From here, a pillar of light connects the individual to a divine reality beyond. The experience is so magnificent that words fail; the only proof is the grace of God that made the vision possible.

translit: turiyamalaimēluḷatōr cōtivaḷa nāṭu tōṉṟumatil aiyarnaṭam ceyyumaṇi vīṭu teriyumatu kaṇṭavarkaḷ kāṇiluyi rōṭu cettavar eḻuvāreṉṟu kaittāḷam pōṭu.
translation: On Turiyamalai is a flourishing land of light. A beautiful hall where the Lord dances appears in it. Those who see it will witness that the dead rise again with life. Clap your hands to this!
commentary: On the mountain of turīya, the state beyond waking, dreaming and deep sleep, lies a land of light, and in it the jewelled house where the Lord dances. Vallalar declares plainly that the dead will rise alive, and calls for hands to clap in joy at this victory over death.

translit: collāl aḷappariya cōtivarai mītu tūyaturi yappatiyil nēyamaṟai ōtu ellāmcey vallacittar tammaiuṟum pōtu iṟantāreḻuvāreṉṟupuṟantāraiūtu.
translation: On the mountain of light, immeasurable by words, is the pure city of Turiya which the beloved Vedas praise. When you reach the all-powerful Siddhars there, blow the purantharai horn, for the dead will rise.
commentary: Again pointing to the superconscious state of turiya, Vallalar calls it a "city of light" where perfected masters, known as siddhars, reside. These beings possess supreme power over life and death. The act of blowing the purantharai, a victory horn, signals that arriving in their presence means witnessing the final triumph over mortality.

translit: ciṟpotuvum poṟpotuvum nāṉaṟiya lāccu cittarkaḷum muttarkaḷum pēcuvateṉ pēccu iṟpakarumivvulakil eṉṉaiiṉi ēccu eṉpiṟavit tuṉpamelām iṉṟōṭē pōccu.
translation: I have come to know both the Chir Podu and the Por Podu. My speech is now what the Siddhars and the liberated ones speak. Who in this world can mock me now? All the suffering of my birth has ended today.
commentary: Vallalar declares a personal transformation. He has realized both the Chir Podu, the inner space of pure consciousness, and the Por Podu, the corresponding universal expanse of divine light. This union has made his words one with the speech of the siddhars and has completely ended the cycle of suffering tied to birth. His confidence is absolute; worldly mockery can no longer touch him.

translit: valatucoṉṉa pērkaḷukku vantatuvāyt tāḻvu maṟṟavaraic cērntavarkkum vantatalait tāḻvu valatupujam āṭanampāl vantataruḷ vāḻvu maṟṟunamaic cūḻntavarkkum vantatunal vāḻvu.
translation: Those who proclaimed what is "right" have been brought to humiliation; those who sided with them have also been brought to shame. As my right shoulder quivers, a life of grace has come to us, and a good life has also come to those who surround us.
commentary: Vallalar addresses the real-world opposition he faced from religious authorities. He states that the arrival of divine grace has vindicated him and humbled his critics. The quivering of his right shoulder is a traditional sign of an auspicious event, confirming that a blessed life has dawned for him and for his entire community.

translit: ampalattil eṅkaḷaiyar āṭiyanal lāṭṭam aṉpoṭutu tittavaruk kāṉatucol lāṭṭam vampucoṉṉa pērkaḷukku vantatumal lāṭṭam vantatalai yāṭṭamiṉṟi vantatupal lāṭṭam.
translation: The fine dance our Lord danced in the Ambalam brought verbal mastery to those who lovingly praised it. For those who spoke idle gossip, it brought a struggle. Instead of a nod of approval, they were met with mockery.
commentary: The dance of God in the sacred hall, or Ambalam, is a core symbol of divine action in the world. Vallalar explains that this single reality produces opposite effects based on one's attitude. For the faithful and loving, it grants inspiration and mastery of speech. For the cynical and gossiping, it brings only conflict and shame.

translit: nāttikamcol kiṉṟavartam nākkumuṭai nākku nākkuruci koḷḷuvatum nāṟiyapiṇ ṇākku cīrttipeṟum ampalavar cīrpukaṉṟa vākku celvākku nalvākku tēvartiru vākku.
translation: The tongues of those who speak atheism are stinking tongues. What their tongues savor is foul oil-cake. The speech that praises the glory of the famed Lord of the Ambalam is influential speech, good speech, the sacred speech of God.
commentary: The words we speak reflect and create our spiritual state. Atheistic speech is spiritually dead, like a rotting tongue tasting spoiled food. In contrast, speech that praises God is alive, powerful, and participates in the divine nature itself.
NOTES
Note 345

tamil: இப்பெரிய விவ்வுலகில் - முதற்பதிப்பு., ச. மு. க. பதிப்பு.
translit: ipperiya vivvulakil - mutaṟpatippu., ca. mu. ka. patippu.
translation: ipperiya vivvulakil — reading of the first edition and the S. Mu. Ka. edition.

translit: aruṭcōti āṉēṉeṉṟu aṟaiyappā muracu aruḷāṭci peṟṟēṉeṉṟu aṟaiyappā muracu maruṭcārpu tīrntēṉeṉṟu aṟaiyappā muracu maraṇanta virntēṉeṉṟu aṟaiyappā muracu.
translation: Beat the drum and announce: I have become the Grace-Light. Beat the drum and announce: I have obtained the reign of Grace. Beat the drum and announce: I am free from all dependence on delusion. Beat the drum and announce: I have escaped death.
commentary: These are declarations of an accomplished spiritual fact. Vallalar announces that he has fully realized the state he has been seeking: he has become one with the Grace-Light, achieved rule over his own being through grace, and conquered both delusion and physical death.

sections.title: O King of the Sacred Hall

translit: civaciva kajamuka kaṇanā tā civakaṇa vantita kuṇanī tā.
translation: Siva! Siva! O elephant-faced Lord of the Ganas! O You of virtuous qualities, praised by Siva's celestial hosts!
commentary: This is a traditional opening invocation to Ganesha, the elephant-headed deity. As the remover of obstacles, he is often honored at the beginning of a new undertaking. Here he is praised as the lord of the Ganas (Siva's celestial attendants) who themselves worship him.

translit: civaciva civaciva tattuva pōtā civakuru paraciva caṇmuka nātā.
translation: Siva! Siva! Siva! Siva! O Teacher of the ultimate truth! O divine Guru, Supreme Siva, six-faced Lord!
commentary: After Ganesha, the invocation turns to Murugan, the six-faced Lord and teacher of the ultimate truth, framed by the repeated cry "Siva, Siva." As in the traditional order of worship, these opening names lead the way to the One praised in the rest of the song, the King of the sacred Ambalam.

translit: ampalat taracē arumarun tē āṉantat tēṉē aruḷvirun tē.
translation: O King of the sacred hall! O rare panacea! O honey of bliss! O feast of grace!
commentary: Here the song names its subject: the King of the sacred Ambalam. God is called the rare medicine for every ill, the honey of bliss and the feast of grace. The images are of healing and nourishment: God is what the soul needs to be well and full.

translit: potunaṭat taracē puṇṇiya ṉē pulavare lāmpukaḻ kaṇṇiya ṉē.
translation: O King of the universal dance! O sacred one! O esteemed one praised by all the sages!
commentary: God is addressed as the cosmic dancer, whose creative energy is the source of the universe. This dance is the very activity that brings all of creation into being, sustains it, and finally dissolves it. The sages and poets who praise him are those who have perceived this truth.

translit: malaitaru makaḷē maṭamayi lē matimuka amutē iḷaṅkuyi lē.
translation: O daughter of the mountain! O graceful peacock! O moon-faced nectar! O young cuckoo!
commentary: After addressing the masculine aspect of God, the prayer immediately turns to the divine feminine. The Goddess is praised with images of natural grace and life-giving sweetness: a peacock, a cuckoo, and nectar itself. This fluid shift shows that for Vallalar, the masculine and feminine principles are two inseparable faces of the one reality.

translit: āṉantak koṭiyē iḷampiṭi yē aṟputat tēṉē malaimā ṉē.
translation: O vine of bliss, O young female elephant, O wondrous honey, O mountain deer.
commentary: The address to the Goddess continues with images that describe the experience of her presence. She is a "vine of bliss," suggesting that joy grows and spreads from her. As a "young elephant" she has a gentle majesty, and as "wondrous honey" she is the taste of overwhelming spiritual sweetness.

translit: civaciva civaciva ciṉmaya tējā civacun tarakuñ citanaṭa rājā.
translation: Siva, Siva, Siva, Siva! O splendor of pure consciousness, O beautiful Siva, King of the dance with the uplifted foot.
commentary: Repeating "Siva" is a powerful devotional practice, used to focus the mind entirely on God. Vallalar defines Siva as the "splendor of pure consciousness," identifying God as the very light of awareness itself. The "uplifted foot" refers to the classic pose of the dancing Siva, a symbol of liberation and grace for the soul.

translit: paṭaṉa vivēka parampara vētā naṭaṉa capēca citampara nātā.
translation: O wisdom discerning the recited Word, O Veda of the eternal lineage, O Lord of the Hall of Dance, O Master of Chidambaram.
commentary: The divine is presented here as the ultimate source of all knowledge. God is both the subject of the holy texts (Vedas) and the very wisdom that understands their inner meaning. The dance takes place in Chidambaram, which is a famous temple but also, mystically, the sacred space within one's own consciousness.

translit: aripira mātiyar tēṭiya nātā arakara civaciva āṭiya pātā.
translation: O Lord sought by Vishnu, Brahma, and others! Hara, Hara, Siva, Siva! O dancing Foot!
commentary: This verse establishes Siva as the supreme God, sought even by other great deities like Brahma the creator and Vishnu the preserver. The phrase "Hara, Hara, Siva, Siva" is an ecstatic cry of surrender. By focusing on the "dancing Foot," the verse points to the source of divine grace, which is traditionally believed to flow from the feet of the Lord to the devoted seeker.

translit: antaṇa aṅkaṇa ampara pōkā ampala nampara ampikai pākā.
translation: O gracious One, O beautiful-eyed Lord, O enjoyer of the cosmic space, O our Lord of the sacred Hall, O you who have the Goddess as your other half.
commentary: Each name here reveals a different aspect of God's nature. He is gracious and beautiful (aṅkaṇa), he pervades all of cosmic space, and he is inseparable from the Goddess, his divine feminine counterpart. This portrays a God who is both personal and cosmic, beautiful and all-encompassing.

translit: ampara vimpa citampara nātā añcita rañcita kuñcita pātā.
translation: O Lord of Chidambaram, the form within the expanse! O One with the beautiful, pleasing, lifted foot!
commentary: God is paradoxically both the infinite, formless space of consciousness (Chidambaram) and the specific, beautiful form that appears within that space. Vallalar focuses again on the dancer's lifted foot (kuñcita pātā), an image that signifies release from worldly bonds and the source of divine grace.

translit: tantira mantira yantirapātā caṅkara caṅkara caṅkara nātā.
translation: O One whose feet are Tantra, Mantra, and Yantra! O Shankara, Shankara, Shankara, Lord!
commentary: The various tools of spiritual practice, Tantra (esoteric systems), Mantra (sacred sounds), and Yantra (mystical diagrams), are not separate from God. Vallalar sees them all as originating from the divine feet, the very foundation of the spiritual path. The verse ends with a repetitive chant of Shankara, a name for Siva meaning 'the auspicious one.'

translit: kaṉaka citampara kaṅkara purahara aṉaka parampara caṅkara harahara.
translation: O Golden Chidambaram, bringer of good, destroyer of the cities! O pure, supreme Shankara, Hara Hara!
commentary: God holds what seem to be opposite qualities in perfect balance. He is the precious 'Golden Chidambaram' and the bringer of good (Shankara), but also the fearsome destroyer of the three cities (pura-hara), a classic image of Siva destroying evil and illusion. The ecstatic chant Hara Hara invokes this complete power.

translit: cakala kalāṇṭa carācara kāraṇa cakuṇa civāṇṭa parāpara pūraṇa.
translation: O Cause of all that moves and is still in every manifested universe! O supreme Fullness, the formed universe of Siva!
commentary: God is the origin of the entire cosmos, the cause behind everything, both animate (cara, that which moves) and inanimate (acara, that which is still). Beyond being the cause, God is also the supreme fullness (parāpara pūraṇam) that constitutes the manifested universe itself.

translit: ikkarai kaṭantiṭil akkarai yē iruppatu citampara carkkarai yē.
translation: If you cross this shore, the other shore is the sweetness of Chidambaram itself.
commentary: This simple verse offers a deep promise about liberation. "This shore" represents our ordinary life of struggle, while "the other shore" is spiritual freedom. Vallalar says this freedom is the pure sweetness (sarkarai, sugar) of Chidambaram, the inner space of divine consciousness. The goal is an experience of overwhelming, delicious bliss.

translit: eṉṉuyir uṭampoṭu cittama tē iṉippatu naṭarāja puttamu tē.
translation: O fresh nectar of Natarajan, you sweeten my very life, body, and consciousness.
commentary: The experience of God is a sweetness that infuses and transforms every aspect of one's being. The "fresh nectar of Natarajan" (Siva as Lord of the Dance) is felt in one's soul (uyir), physical body (uḍampu), and consciousness (cittam). It is a complete saturation with divine bliss.

translit: aiyar tiruccapai āṭaka mē āṭutal āṉanta nāṭaka mē.
translation: O pure gold of the Master's sacred assembly, the dancing is a drama of bliss.
commentary: The "sacred assembly" (tiruccapai) is the space of consciousness where God is present, and Vallalar sees it as precious as pure gold (āṭakam). The activity within this space, God's dance, is an "ānanda nāṭakam," a play of pure bliss. This suggests that the entire cosmic process is a joyful, divine performance.

translit: uttara ñāṉa citampara mē cittie lāntarum amparamē.
translation: O Uttara Jnana Chidambaram, O expanse that grants all siddhis!
commentary: Uttara Jnana Chidambaram, the 'Northern Chidambaram of Wisdom', is the name Vallalar gave to Vadalur, where he raised the Sathya Gnana Sabai. He hails it as the expanse that grants every siddhi: the place on earth where the space of Grace is opened to all.

translit: ampala vāciva mātē vā vampala vāviṅku vāvā vā.
translation: O one of the Ambalam, Siva, Mahadeva! O fragrant one, come, come, come here.
commentary: This is an intimate, urgent call to God, who is addressed by the classic names Siva and Mahadeva (the Great God). The repetition of "come, come, come" expresses a deep longing for the divine presence, felt to be fragrant and dwelling within the Ambalam (the sacred expanse).

translit: naṭarājaṉ ellārkkum nallava ṉē nallae lāmceya vallava ṉē.
translation: Natarajan is good to everyone; he is capable of doing all that is good.
commentary: A simple, deep trust in God's nature is declared here. The divine, called Natarajan, is seen as fundamentally good to everyone and as the source of all good in the world.

translit: āṉanta nāṭakam kaṇṭō mē - para māṉanta pōṉakam koṇṭō mē.
translation: We have witnessed the drama of bliss! We have consumed the meal of supreme bliss!
commentary: The experience of God is more than a vision; it is a form of deep nourishment. The devotee first witnesses the "drama of bliss" and then "consumes" that bliss like a meal, showing that it has become an inseparable part of one's being.

translit: cakaḷa upakaḷa niṭkaḷa nātā ukaḷa catataḷa maṅkaḷa pātā.
translation: O Lord of the sakala, upakala, and nishkala states! O You with auspicious feet upon the joyous hundred-petaled lotus!
commentary: God is praised here as being present in every possible state of existence. He is sakala (with a specific form), niṣkaḷa (completely formless), and upakaḷa (a mix of form and formlessness). This means we can connect with the divine in whatever way is accessible to us, as God is simultaneously concrete and abstract, visible and invisible.

translit: cantata mumciva caṅkara pajaṉam caṅkitam eṉpatu caṟcaṉa vacaṉam.
translation: The virtuous say that true music is the constant devotional singing of Siva Shankara.
commentary: The wise and virtuous declare that true music (saṅgītam) is the devotional singing (bhajanam) of God's names. All other music is secondary; the highest purpose of art is to connect the soul to the divine.

translit: caṅkara mumciva mātē vā eṅkaḷai āṭkoḷa vāvā vā.
translation: O Shankara, O Siva, O Mahadeva! Come, come, come to accept us as Your own.
commentary: This verse is a passionate and urgent plea for grace. By calling on God by His various names, the devotee expresses a deep longing to be accepted into His care. The repetition of "come, come, come" transforms the teaching into a heartfelt prayer.

translit: arakara civaciva mātē vā aruḷamu tamtara vāvā vā.
translation: Harahara, Sivashiva, O Mahadeva! Come, come, come to give the nectar of grace.
commentary: Hara Hara, Siva Siva, great God (Mahadeva): the familiar cries of praise lead to a single plea. Come, come, come, and give the nectar of grace. The triple "come" carries the urgency of the longing.

translit: naṭaṉaci kāmaṇi navamaṇi yē tiṭaṉaka māmaṇi civamaṇi yē.
translation: Crest-jewel of dance, O nine-gem jewel! Great gem of the mighty mountain, O gem of Siva!
commentary: God is called a jewel again and again: crest-jewel of the dance, jewel of the nine gems, great jewel of the mighty mountain, jewel of Siva. Every precious thing the world knows is gathered into names for God.

translit: naṭamiṭum ampala naṉmaṇi yē puṭamiṭu cempala poṉmaṇi yē.
translation: O good gem of the dancing hall! O golden gem of perfectly refined gold!
commentary: God is the good gem of the dancing Hall and gold refined to perfection. Refined gold has passed through fire and lost every impurity. The image suits the One who is pure, without any trace of malam.

translit: uvaṭṭātu cittikkum uḷḷamu tē teviṭṭātu tittikkum teḷḷamu tē.
translation: O inner ambrosia that grants attainment and never cloys, O clear ambrosia that is sweet and never satiates.
commentary: Worldly sweetness cloys; take too much and it turns to aversion. The nectar within never does. It grants every attainment, and the more it is tasted the sweeter it grows. Vallalar sets the pleasures that tire beside the one sweetness that never ends.

translit: naṭarāja vaḷḷalai nāṭuta lē namtoḻi lāmviḷai yāṭuta lē.
translation: Seeking the generous Lord Nataraja is our one work and our one play.
commentary: Seeking Nataraja, the generous Lord, is all our work, and it is also all our play. For Vallalar, seeking God is life's whole work and its joy at once.

translit: aruṭpotu naṭamiṭu tāṇṭava ṉē aruṭperuñ cōtieṉ āṇṭava ṉē.
translation: O You who dance the Tandava in the universal space of Grace! O ArutPerunJothi, my Lord!
commentary: God dances the cosmic dance (tāṇṭavam) in the common space of grace, open to all. Vallalar ends the line with the name he uses most in the Sixth Thirumurai: ArutPerunJothi, my Lord.

translit: naṭarāja māṇikkam oṉṟatu vē naṇṇutal āṇippoṉ maṉṟatu vē.
translation: The one true ruby is Nataraja. The place to attain him is the hall of pure gold.
commentary: The most precious thing in existence is God, who is envisioned as Nataraja, the divine cosmic dancer. Vallalar says the place to find this ultimate treasure is the "hall of pure gold," a reference to the temple at Chidambaram and, more importantly, the inner sanctuary of one's own being.

translit: naṭarāja palamatu nampala mē naṭamāṭu vatutiru ampala mē.
translation: The strength of Nataraja is our strength. The place where he dances is the sacred Ambalam.
commentary: All our power and vitality are not truly our own; they are expressions of God's infinite strength. The cosmic dance of creation unfolds in the sacred space called the Ampalam (hall), which is both the universe and the field of our own awareness.

translit: naṭarājar pāṭṭē naṟumpāṭṭu ñālattār pāṭṭellām veṟumpāṭṭu.
translation: Nataraja's song is the only sweet song. The songs of the people of the world are all empty songs.
commentary: The only "song" with real substance and sweetness is the vibration of divine reality. Compared to this eternal melody, all human creations and worldly pursuits are empty and fleeting.

translit: citamparap pāṭṭē tiruppāṭṭu jīvarkaḷ pāṭṭellām teruppāṭṭu.
translation: The song of Chidambaram is the sacred song. The songs of all souls are mere street songs.
commentary: The song originating from Citāmparam, the sacred space of pure consciousness, is holy. In contrast, the songs produced by individual souls (jīvarkaḷ), when caught up in worldly life, are as common and insignificant as noise on a busy street.

translit: ampalap pāṭṭē aruṭpāṭṭu allāta pāṭṭellām maruṭpāṭṭu.
translation: The song of the Ambalam is the song of grace. All other songs are songs of delusion.
commentary: The vibration that emanates from the Ampalam (the divine hall) is the very expression of grace. Any other focus, any other mental "song," is a source of delusion that keeps one bound to illusion.

translit: ampala vāṇaṇai nāṭiṉa ṉē avaṉaṭi yāroṭum kūṭiṉa ṉē.
translation: I sought the Lord of the Cosmic Hall; I joined with his devotees.
commentary: The spiritual path has two essential parts: a personal, inner seeking for God, the "Lord of the Cosmic Hall," and an outer joining with the community of fellow seekers who share the same devotion.

translit: tampata māmpukaḻ pāṭiṉa ṉē tantaṉa eṉṟukūt tāṭiṉa ṉē.
translation: I sang the glory of his holy feet; I danced to the beat of 'tantana'.
commentary: The response to divine grace is spontaneous and ecstatic. Vallalar expresses this through singing about God's feet, a symbol of divine refuge, and dancing with the joyful certainty that grace has been given. The experience is an overflowing celebration.

translit: nāṉcoṉṉa pāṭalum kēṭṭā rē ñāṉa citampara nāṭṭā rē.
translation: The Lord of Gnana Chidambaram even listened to the song I sang.
commentary: There is a deep sense of wonder and intimacy here: the supreme Lord of Gnana Chidambaram (the Chidambaram of wisdom) actually listened to his song. His prayer is heard and received.

translit: iṉittuyar paṭamāṭṭēṉ viṭṭē ṉē eṉkuru mēlāṇai iṭṭē ṉē.
translation: I will suffer sorrow no more; I have let it go. I have sworn an oath upon my Guru.
commentary: This is a powerful declaration of freedom from sorrow. The suffering is gone and actively renounced through a solemn oath sworn on the Guru. It marks a point of no return, a conscious decision to live in a new state of being free from pain.

translit: iṉippāṭu paṭamāṭṭēṉ viṭṭē ṉē eṉṉappaṉ mēlāṇai iṭṭē ṉē.
translation: I will struggle no more; I have let it go. I have sworn an oath upon my Father.
commentary: Reinforcing the previous verse, Vallalar now vows to end all struggle, this time swearing on his Father, God. By letting go of both sorrow and struggle, he empties himself of the burdens that define ordinary life, making space for the divine.

translit: caṉmārkkam naṉmārkkam naṉmārkkam cakamārkkam tuṉmārkkam tuṉmārkkam.
translation: Sanmarkkam is the good path, the good path. The worldly path is the evil path, the evil path.
commentary: Vallalar draws a sharp, uncompromising line between two ways of life. Sanmarkkam is the true path of compassion and oneness that he teaches. He contrasts it with the sakamārkkam (the worldly path), which is focused on selfish desires. The emphatic repetition insists there is no middle ground.

translit: nātānta nāṭṭukku nāyaka rē naṭarāja rēcapā nāyaka rē.
translation: Oh Lord of the land of Nādānta! Oh Nataraja, Lord of the Sabhā!
commentary: This verse addresses God with two great titles. Nādānta refers to the ultimate spiritual state where the inner, mystic sound of creation resolves into silence. Nataraja, the cosmic dancer, is the Lord of the Sabhā (Hall of Consciousness). Both names describe God as the supreme master of reality itself.

translit: nāṉcollum itukēḷīr cattiya mē naṭarāja eṉilvarum nittiya mē.
translation: Listen to what I say; it is the absolute truth. If you say 'Nataraja', eternity itself will come.
commentary: This is a promise of immense power. Vallalar insists that simply uttering the name Nataraja with sincere feeling is enough to bring forth nittiyam (eternity). The divine name contains the very presence of the reality it represents, making liberation accessible through simple, heartfelt devotion.

translit: nallōr ellārkkum capāpati yē nalvaram īyum tayāniti yē.
translation: Sabhāpati is for all good people; he is the treasure of compassion who grants good boons.
commentary: God’s grace is available to all good-hearted people, regardless of their background. His fundamental nature is compassion (dayānidhi, a treasure of compassion), and he freely gives blessings.

translit: naṭarājar tamnaṭam naṉṉaṭa mē naṭampuri kiṉṟatum eṉṉiṭa mē.
translation: Nataraja's dance is the supreme dance. And he performs that dance right here within me.
commentary: The cosmic dance that creates and sustains the universe is happening right here inside the individual. This verse brings the vast, universal divine into the most personal and intimate space of one's own being.

translit: civakāma vallikku māppiḷḷai yē tiruvāḷaṉ nāṉavaṉ cīrppiḷḷai yē.
translation: He is the bridegroom for Sivakama Valli. He is the Lord of Grace, and I am his esteemed child.
commentary: Vallalar describes his relationship with God using the tender language of family. God is the Lord of Grace, and Vallalar sees himself as God's own child, cherished and esteemed. This shifts the devotee's position from a distant servant to a beloved member of the divine household.

translit: civakāma valliyaic cērntava ṉē cittellām ceytiṭat tērntava ṉē.
translation: He is the one who united with Sivakama Valli. He is the one skilled in performing all the siddhis.
commentary: The source of God's limitless power, including the ability to perform miracles (siddhis), flows from his union with the divine feminine. This joining of consciousness (Siva) with grace and energy (Sivakama Valli) represents a state of perfect wholeness from which all possibilities emerge.

translit: iṟavā varamtaru naṟcapai yē eṉamaṟai pukaḻvatu ciṟcapai yē.
translation: The good assembly that grants the boon of deathlessness is the Chitrambalam, which the scriptures praise.
commentary: The true place that grants the gift of deathlessness is an inner space. Vallalar identifies this sacred place as the Chitrambalam, the hall of pure consciousness within oneself.

translit: eṉiru kaṇṇuḷ iruntava ṉē iṟavā taruḷum maruntava ṉē.
translation: He is the one who resides within my two eyes. He is the medicine that grants the grace of deathlessness.
commentary: God's presence is experienced as residing within one's own eyes. This divine presence is the very "medicine" that bestows immortality, a direct and tangible grace.

translit: ciṟcapai appaṉai uṟṟē ṉē cittie lāmceyap peṟṟē ṉē.
translation: I have attained the Father in the Chitrambalam. I have received the power to perform all the siddhis.
commentary: By uniting with God within the inner hall of consciousness (Chitrambalam), one gains mastery over reality itself. This attainment brings with it the ability to perform all siddhis (supernatural powers).

translit: ampala vāṇartam aṭiyava rē aruḷara cāḷmaṇi muṭiyava rē.
translation: The devotees of the Lord of the Ambalam are the ones crowned with gems, ruling the kingdom of grace.
commentary: This verse redefines true royalty. The real rulers, wearing crowns of gems, are the devotees of God, who preside over a spiritual kingdom of grace, not a worldly one.

translit: aruṭperuñcōtiyaik kaṇṭē ṉē āṉantat teḷḷamu tuṇṭē ṉē.
translation: I have seen the Vast Grace-Light! I have drunk the clear ambrosia of bliss!
commentary: The vision of the Divine is an experience of overwhelming light, the ArutPerunJothi or Vast Grace-Light. This encounter is seen and felt and tasted, like drinking a pure ambrosia that fills the soul with bliss.

translit: iruṭperu māyaiyai viṇṭē ṉē ellāmcey cittiyaik koṇṭē ṉē.
translation: I have dispelled the great darkness of māyā! I have obtained the siddhi that can do all things!
commentary: The divine light is so powerful that it completely dissolves māyā, the cosmic illusion that makes us see the world as separate from God. Once this illusion is gone, all limitations vanish, and one gains the siddhi, the power to accomplish anything.

translit: karuṇā nitiyē kuṇaniti yē katimā nitiyē kalāniti yē.
translation: O treasure of compassion! O treasure of virtue! O great treasure of refuge! O treasure of all arts!
commentary: This is a hymn of praise, calling on God by naming what He embodies. God is more than compassionate or virtuous; He is the very source, the "treasure," of compassion, virtue, safety, and all creative arts.

translit: taruṇā patiyē civapati yē taṉimā patiyē capāpati yē.
translation: O youthful Lord! O Lord Siva! O singular, great Lord! O Sabapathi!
commentary: Vallalar addresses God with names that are both personal and traditional. He is the ever-youthful Lord, the great Lord Siva (the Auspicious One), and Sabapathi (Lord of the Hall), connecting his vision to the ancient symbol of the dancing God at Chidambaram.

translit: karuṇā nitiyē capāpati yē katimā nitiyē pacupati yē.
translation: O Treasure of compassion, O Sabhapati! O great treasure of refuge, O Pasupati!
commentary: The divine quality of compassion is linked to God’s identity as Sabhapati, the Lord of Consciousness, while his role as a refuge is tied to his name Pasupati, the Lord of all souls (pasu). This connects the abstract idea of a caring God to the specific being who presides over both consciousness itself and every living creature.

translit: capāpati pātam tapōpra cātam tayāniti pōtam catōtaya vētam.
translation: The feet of Sabhapati are the grace of spiritual discipline. The wisdom of the Treasure of Compassion is the Veda of eternal dawning.
commentary: Surrendering to God is the highest fruit of any spiritual discipline. This verse also makes a bold claim: the true sacred scripture (Veda) is the living wisdom that flows directly from the God of compassion, a truth that is always dawning anew within the soul.

translit: karuṇām paravara karaciva pavapava aruṇām paratara harahara civaciva.
translation: O Excellent One clothed in compassion, O auspicious Doer, Bhava, Bhava! O Wearer of the dawn-red expanse, Hara, Hara, Siva, Siva!
commentary: This verse is a powerful, chant-like invocation using traditional names for Lord Siva. Bhava means the one who brings all things into being, while Hara is the one who dissolves them. Siva means the auspicious and pure one. By repeating these names, Vallalar evokes the totality of God's power, from creation to dissolution, framing it all within an essential nature of compassion.

translit: kaṉakā karapura haracira karatara karuṇā karapara curavara harahara.
translation: O mine of gold, Destroyer of cities, Holder of the head in hand! O Supreme One, an ocean of compassion, Chief of the gods, Hara, Hara!
commentary: Here, imagery of immense power is fused with infinite mercy. "Mine of gold" points to God as the source of all value. "Destroyer of cities" and "Holder of the head" are traditional descriptions of Siva's awesome power, used to destroy ego and illusion. Even in this fearsome aspect, he is an "ocean of compassion," showing that God's ultimate purpose is always rooted in grace.

translit: kaṉaka capāpati pacupati navapati aṉaka umāpati atipati civapati.
translation: Golden Sabhapati, Pasupati, the New Lord. The Flawless One, consort of Uma, the Supreme Lord, Lord Siva.
commentary: The names here connect God to specific roles and places. He is Sabhapati (Lord of the sacred dancing hall at Chidambaram) and Pasupati (Lord of all souls). By also calling him the "New Lord," Vallalar suggests that this ancient God is being revealed in a fresh, immediate way.

translit: vētānta parāmpara jayajaya nātānta naṭāmpara jayajaya.
translation: Hail, hail, supreme one beyond Vedanta! Hail, hail, dancer in the expanse beyond Nada!
commentary: God is beyond what can be captured by human thought or systems. The divine reality surpasses even Vedanta (the highest school of philosophy) and Nada (the primordial sound from which the universe is born).

translit: ēkānta carvēta camōtama yōkānta naṭēca namōnama.
translation: O solitary one, the highest tranquility of all the Vedas! Salutations, salutations to the Lord of Dance, the culmination of Yoga!
commentary: The ultimate goal of studying scripture (Vedas) is the tranquility found in God, and the final attainment of spiritual practice (Yoga) is union with Him. Vallalar identifies this supreme state with the Lord of the Dance himself.

translit: ātāmpara āṭaka aticaya pātāmpuja nāṭaka jayajaya.
translation: Hail, hail to the wondrous dance of the magnificent golden lotus feet!
commentary: This is a simple, direct expression of loving surrender. The "wondrous dance" is all of God's activity in the cosmos, and the "lotus feet" are the traditional symbol for the source of divine grace, the place where a devotee can find shelter.

translit: pōtānta purēca civākama nātānta naṭēca namōnama.
translation: O Lord of the City, the culmination of knowledge and the Sivagamas! Salutations, salutations to you, Lord of Dance, the culmination of Nada!
commentary: God is the single reality that underlies all paths to truth, whether through knowledge (bodha), sacred texts (Sivagamas), or the mystical experience of primal sound (Nada). He is the destination where all these different streams of wisdom meet.

translit: jāla kōlakaṉa kāmpara cāyaka kāla kālavaṉa kāmpara nāyaka.
translation: O you who recline in the golden expanse of the web of worlds! O Lord of the beautiful expanse, the Death of Death!
commentary: The Lord is the reality that sustains the vast, interconnected network of all worlds, while also being the timeless principle that conquers death itself. To call God the "Death of Death" means he is the eternal reality beyond all cycles of creation and destruction.

translit: nāta pālacu lōcaṉa varttaṉa jāta jālavi mōcaṉa nirttaṉa.
translation: O enhancer of the Nāda, bearer of the crescent moon, possessor of the divine eye! O dancer who brings liberation from the web of birth!
commentary: The divine dancer is the one who intensifies the primal cosmic sound (Nāda) and liberates beings from the endless cycle of birth and death. The dance is more than a cosmic spectacle; it is the very act of grace that sets souls free.

translit: catapari catavupa catamata vitapava citapari katapata civaciva civaciva.
translation: O you who become manifold as the true fullness, the true path, the true doctrine! O fullness of consciousness, O transcendent state! Siva, Siva, Siva, Siva.
commentary: God is the destination and the path and the teaching that leads there. This verse describes a divine reality that is simultaneously the goal (the fullness of consciousness), the way to reach it, and the wisdom that guides us, all encompassed by the holy name Siva.

translit: arakara varacupa karakara pavapava cirapura curapara civaciva civaciva.
translation: Hara, Hara! O giver of boons and auspiciousness, Hara, Hara, Bhava, Bhava! O one from the city upon the head, O supreme among the celestials! Siva, Siva, Siva, Siva.
commentary: This verse is a powerful chant, calling on God by several traditional names. Hara means the one who removes suffering, while Bhava means the one who simply is, the source of all existence. The reference to a "city upon the head" places this supreme being at the highest point of spiritual realization, accessible within our own consciousness.

translit: upala ciratala cupakaṇa vaṅkaṇa cupala karatala kaṇapaṇa kaṅkaṇa.
translation: O one with a jeweled head, worshipped by your auspicious attendants! O one whose palm grants auspicious fruits, who wears a bracelet of clustered serpent hoods!
commentary: Vallalar paints a vivid picture of God's divine form, combining majesty and power. The serpents worn as a bracelet symbolize complete control over cosmic energy and the cycle of life and death, while the hand that offers "auspicious fruits" shows this same power is used to bestow blessings.

translit: apayava ratakara talapuri kāraṇa upayapa ratapata parapari pūraṇa.
translation: O Prime Cause, who acts with hands showing the gestures of protection and boons! O supreme, all-pervading fullness, whose two feet perform the divine dance!
commentary: God is the ultimate source of the universe, the "Prime Cause." His divine nature is expressed through two key actions: the hand gestures that signal "do not fear" and "I will grant your wishes," and the cosmic dance that sustains the universe. The dancing feet are more than movement; they represent the divine play that both creates and offers liberation.

translit: akara:u karacupa karavara ciṉakara takarava karanava puracira tiṉakara.
translation: O A and U, Maker of auspiciousness, Maker of the sign of boons, Ta and Va, Head of the nine realms, O Sun!
commentary: The divine is identified with the fundamental sounds of language itself. In this mystical view, certain letters are symbols and are the vibrational essence of cosmic principles. A and U are the first two components of AUM (or Om), the sacred sound from which all creation is said to emerge. By calling God these letters, Vallalar points to the divine as the very source code of reality.

translit: vakaraci karatiṉa karacaci karapura makaraa karavara purahara harahara.
translation: O Va, Si, Sun, Moon, and City! O Ma, A, and City of Boons! Hara! Hara! Hara!
commentary: This verse continues to invoke the divine through sacred syllables, which are like cosmic connection points. Si and Va are the core of Na-Ma-Si-Va-Ya, the most revered mantra for Lord Siva. Hara is another name for Siva, meaning 'the one who removes' our suffering, illusion, and ego. Repeating "Hara, Hara, Hara" is a powerful, devotional chant of surrender.

translit: paramaman tiracaka ḷākaṉa karaṇā paṭaṉatan tiranika mākama caraṇā.
translation: O Supreme Mantra, Embodiment of All, First Cause! O Refuge for the recitation, the techniques, the Vedas, and the Agamas!
commentary: The divine is the Supreme Mantra (parama mantra) itself. All the sacred texts like the Vedas and Agamas, and all the spiritual techniques (tantra), are simply paths leading to this ultimate reality. God is presented as the final refuge, the very goal that all religious practices aim for.

translit: aṉantakō ṭikuṇa karakara jolitā akaṇṭavē tacira karatara palitā.
translation: O You who shine with countless billions of radiant virtues, the crown of the undivided Vedas, the very fruit held in the hand!
commentary: This closing praise describes the divine as possessing infinite good qualities, shining with countless virtues. God is the highest truth of the scriptures (Vedas), their "crown." Yet this immense, abstract being is also described as "the very fruit held in the hand," making the ultimate spiritual reward feel immediate, personal, and attainable.

translit: paripūraṇa ñāṉaci tampara patikāraṇa nātapa rampara.
translation: O Perfect Space of Consciousness-Wisdom, Lord, Cause, Primal Sound, the Transcendent-and-Immanent One.
commentary: This verse captures the all-encompassing nature of God. He is the vast, silent space of pure consciousness (cit-ambaram), the source of creation, the first vibration of existence (nāda), and the paradoxical reality that is both inside the world and far beyond it.

translit: civañāṉapa tāṭaka nāṭaka civapōtapa rōkaḷa kūṭaka.
translation: You are the drama of the foot-ornament of Siva-wisdom; you are the union with the supreme world of Siva-realization.
commentary: God is presented here as both the dynamic expression of wisdom and the final state of union. He is the beautiful "drama" of divine insight (Sivajñānam) playing out in the world, and He is also the blissful merging (union) with that divine consciousness (Sivabodham), which is the goal of spiritual life.

translit: cakala lōkapara kāraka vāraka capaḷa yōkacara pūraka tāraka.
translation: You are the supreme agent and remover for all worlds; you are the fulfillment of the essence of fruitful yoga, the liberator.
commentary: God's power is absolute, governing all of creation as its supreme "agent and remover." This cosmic power is also deeply personal; He is the one who makes spiritual disciplines like yoga successful and who finally grants liberation to the seeker.

translit: catva pōtaka tāraṇa taṉmaya catya vētaka pūraṇa ciṉmaya.
translation: You are the teacher of goodness, whose very nature is to be the foundation; you are the revealer of truth, the fullness of pure consciousness.
commentary: God is the source of all that is good and true. He is the teacher of goodness (sattva), the stable foundation of existence, and the one who reveals truth because He is truth itself: a boundless reality made of pure consciousness (cinmaya).

translit: varakē cānta makōtaya kāriya parapā cānta cukōtaya cūriya.
translation: You are the supreme transcendent state, the cause of the great awakening; you are the peace beyond the supreme light, the sun that makes bliss awaken.
commentary: God is the destination and also the means to get there. He is the supreme state of peace beyond all spiritual light, and He is the sun whose rising causes our own inner bliss to awaken.

translit: paḷita tīpaka cōpita pātā laḷita rūpaka stāpita nātā.
translation: O splendidly adorned Feet, a lamp of fruition! O Lord, established in a graceful form!
commentary: This verse focuses on the visible, worshipful form of the divine. God's feet are described as a shining lamp that brings the devotee's spiritual efforts to fruition. This praises the Lord for making himself accessible in a graceful form that can be contemplated.

translit: aṉirtakōpakaru ṇāmpaka nā tā amirta rūpataru ṇāmpuja pā tā.
translation: O Lord, angered by falsehood, with eyes of compassion! O one whose form is nectar, whose feet are tender lotuses!
commentary: God's nature is shown to have two sides: a fierce anger toward falsehood and injustice, and eyes filled with compassion. This anger is a protective response born from love. The verse then praises God's form as being like amṛta (divine nectar) itself.

translit: ampō rukapata arakara kaṅkara campō civaciva civaciva caṅkara.
translation: O one with lotus feet! Hara! Hara! You who bear the Ganga! O Shambhu! Siva, Siva, Siva, Siva! O Shankara!
commentary: This final verse is a devotional chant, pouring out a stream of sacred names for God, identifying the ultimate reality with the divine figure of Siva. Repeating names like Hara (the remover of suffering), Shambhu (the source of good), and especially "Siva, Siva" is an act of worship meant to dissolve the mind in the divine presence.

translit: citampira kācā parampira kā cā citampa rēcā cuyampira kā cā.
translation: O Splendor of Chidambaram! O Supreme Splendor! O Lord of Chidambaram! O Self-Luminous Splendor!
commentary: Chidambaram is a sacred temple town, but for Vallalar it also represents the inner space of pure consciousness. He addresses God as the light that shines both in that holy place and as the supreme, self-generating light of reality itself.

translit: aruṭpira kācam parappira kācam akappira kācam civappira kācam.
translation: The splendor of Grace, the supreme splendor, the inner splendor, the splendor of Siva.
commentary: The divine splendor is many lights: the light of grace, the light of ultimate reality, the light within our own minds, and the light that is Siva. For Vallalar, all these forms of light are one and the same.

translit: naṭappira kācam tavappira kācam navappira kācam civappira kācam.
translation: The splendor of the Dance, the splendor of austerity, the ever-new splendor, the splendor of Siva.
commentary: The divine light manifests in dynamic action (the cosmic Dance of Siva), in focused spiritual practice (tavam, or austerity), and in the freshness of each new moment. All these expressions of splendor are aspects of Siva's own radiant being.

tamil: நாத பரம்பர னே பர - நாத சிதம்பர னே
நாத திகம்பர னே தச - நாத சுதந்தர னே.
translit: nāta parampara ṉē para - nāta citampara ṉē nāta tikampara ṉē taca - nāta cutantara ṉē.
translation: O Supreme Progenitor of Nāda! O Chidambaram of transcendent sound! O Digambara of sound! O independent Master of the ten sounds!
commentary: God is praised as the ultimate source of Nāda, the primordial cosmic sound from which all creation emerges. He is the boundless consciousness (Digambara, literally "clothed in space") where this sound vibrates, and the independent master of all its forms and expressions.

tamil: ஞான நடத்தவ னே பர - ஞானிஇ டத்தவ னே
ஞான வரத்தவ னே சிவ - ஞான புரத்தவ னே.
translit: ñāṉa naṭattava ṉē para - ñāṉii ṭattava ṉē ñāṉa varattava ṉē civa - ñāṉa purattava ṉē.
translation: O Performer of the dance of wisdom! O One who dwells with the supremely wise! O Boon of wisdom! O Resident of the city of Siva-wisdom!
commentary: Wisdom is a concept and a dynamic, living reality. God is the source of this wisdom, enacting it as a dance, dwelling within those who attain it, and granting it as the ultimate gift.

tamil: ஞான சபாபதி யே மறை - நாடு சதாகதி யே
தீன தாயாநிதி யே பர - தேவி உமாபதி யே.
translit: ñāṉa capāpati yē maṟai - nāṭu catākati yē tīṉa tāyāniti yē para - tēvi umāpati yē.
translation: O Lord of the Hall of Wisdom! O eternal refuge sought by the Vedas! O treasure of compassion for the destitute! O Lord of Uma, the supreme Goddess!
commentary: The divine is praised here in several distinct roles. He is the master of the inner space where wisdom dawns, the ultimate goal pointed to by ancient scriptures (Vedas), a fountain of mercy for those in need, and the divine consort of the Goddess Uma.

translit: puttamtarum pōtā vittamtarum tātā nittamtarum pātā cittamtirum pātā.
translation: O Teacher who gives enlightenment! O Giver who gives wealth! O Feet that grant eternity! O Feet from which the mind never turns away!
commentary: The divine provides for every aspect of life, both spiritual and material. This verse praises God as the one who bestows wisdom, provides worldly sustenance, offers eternal existence, and captivates the mind so completely that it finds its final resting place.

note: A separate song in the 1932 edition (numbered 137 in the Tamil source edition).
translit: naṭunāṭi naṭunāṭi naṭamāṭu patiyē naṭarāja naṭarāja naṭarāja nitiyē.
translation: O Lord who dances in the central channel, having sought its center! O Nataraja, Nataraja, Nataraja, the Treasure!
commentary: God dances in the central channel (naṭu nāṭi), the inner path at the center of the body. The triple "Nataraja, Nataraja, Nataraja" is chanted like a mantra. God is named the Treasure, the One found when the seeking reaches the center.

translit: naṭunāṭi yoṭukūṭi naṭamāṭum uruvē naṭarāja naṭarāja naṭarāja kuruvē.
translation: O Form who dances, united with the central channel! O Nataraja, Nataraja, Nataraja, O Guru!
commentary: The Form that dances is united with the central channel: the dance of God is not only in the Hall outside but within the body itself. Nataraja is named three times again, and then Guru. The Lord of the dance is also the inner teacher.

translit: naṭunāṭi iṭaināṭi naṭamāṭum nalamē naṭarāja naṭarāja naṭarāja palamē.
translation: O Excellence who dances in the central channel and the left channel! O Nataraja, Nataraja, Nataraja, O Power!
commentary: Vallalar connects the grand, cosmic dance of Siva as Lord of the Dance (Nataraja) to the subtle energetic pathways within the human body. The dance of creation and dissolution happens in the universe and within us, along channels of life-force like the central channel and the left channel (ida). This inner dance is the source of all power and grace.
NOTES
Note 339

tamil: ஆ பா. பதிப்பைத் தவிர மற்றைப் பதிப்புகள் அனைத்திலும் "அம்பலத்தரசே" முதலாகநாமாவளி தொடங்குகிறது. ஆ. பா. பதிப்பில் மட்டும் இவ்விரண்டு நாமாவளிகளும்முன்வைக்கப் பெற்று "அம்பலத்தரசே" மூன்றாவதாக வைக்கப்பெற்றுள்ளது.இறுக்கம் இரத்தின முதலியார், வேட்டவலம் ஜமீன்தார் அப்பாசாமி பண்டாரியார்இவ்விருவரின் படிகளில் மட்டுமே இவ்விரண்டு நாமாவளிகள் காணப்பெறுவதாயும்,கிடைத்த மற்றைப் படிகளில் இவை இல்லை என்றும், அவற்றில் "அம்பலத்தரசே"என்பதே தொடக்கம் என்றும் ஆ. பா. குறிக்கிறார். இப்பதிப்பில் இவ்விருநாமாவளிகளும் தனியாக எண்ணிடப் பெற்றுத் தனிப்படுத்திக் காட்டப் பெற்றுள்ளன.அம்பலத்தரசே எனத் தொடங்கும் நாமாவளிக்கு இவ்விரண்டையும் காப்பாகக்கொள்ளலாம்.
translit: ā pā. patippait tavira maṟṟaip patippukaḷ aṉaittilum "ampalattaracē" mutalākanāmāvaḷi toṭaṅkukiṟatu. ā. pā. patippil maṭṭum ivviraṇṭu nāmāvaḷikaḷummuṉvaikkap peṟṟu "ampalattaracē" mūṉṟāvatāka vaikkappeṟṟuḷḷatu.iṟukkam irattiṉa mutaliyār, vēṭṭavalam jamīṉtār appācāmi paṇṭāriyārivviruvariṉ paṭikaḷil maṭṭumē ivviraṇṭu nāmāvaḷikaḷ kāṇappeṟuvatāyum,kiṭaitta maṟṟaip paṭikaḷil ivai illai eṉṟum, avaṟṟil "ampalattaracē"eṉpatē toṭakkam eṉṟum ā. pā. kuṟikkiṟār. ippatippil ivvirunāmāvaḷikaḷum taṉiyāka eṇṇiṭap peṟṟut taṉippaṭuttik kāṭṭap peṟṟuḷḷaṉa.ampalattaracē eṉat toṭaṅkum nāmāvaḷikku ivviraṇṭaiyum kāppākakkoḷḷalām.
translation: In all editions except the Ā. Pā. edition, the nāmāvaḷi (the garland of divine names) begins with "ampalattaracē". Only in the Ā. Pā. edition are these two nāmāvaḷis placed at the head, with "ampalattaracē" placed third. That edition states that these two nāmāvaḷis are found only in the copies belonging to Iṟukkam Irattiṉa Mutaliyār and to Appācāmi Paṇṭāriyār, the zamindar of Vēṭṭavalam; that they are absent from the other copies obtained; and that in those copies "am… [the note breaks off here].

translit: cavutaya - ā. pā. patippu.
translation: cavutaya — reading of the Ā. Pā. edition.
Note 341

translit: aṉurta - ca. mu. ka. patippu.
translation: aṉurta — reading of the S. Mu. Ka. Edition.

translit: pōkam cukapōkam civapōkam atunittiyam ēkam civamēkam civamēkam itucattiyam.
translation: Enjoyment, blissful enjoyment, the enjoyment of Siva, that is eternal. The One is Siva, Siva is One, Siva is One, this is the truth.
commentary: The only true and eternal enjoyment is the experience of God (Sivapōkam). All other worldly pleasures are temporary and unsatisfying. The ultimate reality is singular, and that One is Siva; this, Vallalar states, is the absolute truth.

translit: nalamaṅkalam uṟumampala naṭaṉamatu naṭaṉam palanaṉkaruḷ civacaṅkara paṭaṉamatu paṭaṉam.
translation: The dance in the Ambalam that bestows goodness and auspiciousness, that is the true dance. The declaration of Siva Sankara, who grants many good graces, that is the true declaration.
commentary: The only dance that truly matters is the divine vibration in the Ambalam, the inner hall of consciousness, which brings goodness into our lives. Likewise, the only declaration worth hearing is the word of Siva, the source of all grace.

note: A separate song in the 1932 edition (numbered 136 in the Tamil source edition).
translit: cūtumaṉṉum intaiyē cūṭaleṉṉa vintaiyē kōtuviṇṭa cintaiyē kōyilkoṇṭa tantaiyē.
translation: In this state ruled by deceit, what a wonder this adornment is! Oh, mind cleansed of its faults! Oh, Father who has taken it as your temple!
commentary: Vallalar marvels at a spiritual miracle: in a world filled with deceit (sūtu), it is possible for the divine to enter and adorn a soul with grace. The condition is a purified mind, one cleansed of its flaws. When the mind becomes pure, God, the Father, makes it His own temple.

translit: aṉpumuntu cintaiyē ampalaṅkoḷ vintaiyē iṉpameṉpaṉ entaiyē entaitantai tantaiyē.
translation: Oh, mind where love comes first! Oh, marvel of containing the Ambalam! I call it bliss, oh my Father! Oh, Father of my father's father!
commentary: A mind where love takes priority becomes the Ambalam, the sacred space containing God. Vallalar speaks directly to his own mind, realizing that this state is the highest bliss. By calling God "Father of my father's father," he expresses God's timeless nature as the ultimate source of all existence.

translit: ñāṉacitti purattaṉē nātacatti parattaṉē vāṉamotta tarattaṉē vātavittai varattaṉē.
translation: Oh, dweller in the city of wisdom-perfection! Oh, supreme one of Nada and Shakti! Oh, one whose nature is like the vast sky! Oh, bestower of the boon of the art of Vada!
commentary: God is described as the source of all reality and power. He is the master of Nada (the primal sound of creation) and Shakti (the primal energy that animates it). He grants the ultimate alchemical secret of Vada, the science of transforming the physical body into an immortal, divine form. His nature is as vast and limitless as the sky.

translit: nīeṉṉappaṉ allavā niṉakkumiṉṉañ collavā tāyiṉmikka nallavā carvacitti vallavā.
translation: Are you not my Father? Need I say more to you? You are better than a mother, the master of all siddhis.
commentary: This verse expresses a deep, personal intimacy with God. Vallalar speaks with the trust of a child who knows his father understands his heart without needing many words. He finds God's love to be even more perfect and nurturing than a mother's, and this love is backed by mastery over all siddhis (supernatural powers).

translit: palattiltaṉṉam palattilpoṉṉam palattiltuṉṉum nalattaṉē palattilpaṉṉum parattiltuṉṉum parattilmaṉṉum kulattaṉē.
translation: O virtuous one, abounding in the hall of strength, the Golden Hall! O you of a transcendent nature, praised in many scriptures, filling and reigning in the highest realm!
commentary: God's presence is praised as being both immanent and transcendent. He fills the "Golden Hall," which refers simultaneously to the sacred space of the Chidambaram temple and the luminous space of consciousness within a person. At the same time, He is the supreme being who reigns in the highest state, beyond all form.

translit: āyavāya nēyañēya māyañāya vātiyē tūyavāya kāyatēya tōyamēya jōtiyē.
translation: O primordial one of just law beyond illusion, who are both love and the object of knowledge, manifest as the true Word! O Jothi that pervades the waters, you are the very space of the pure, manifest body!
commentary: God is the ultimate reality that is simultaneously love, knowledge, and the very substance of creation. Vallalar sees this divine presence, the Jothi (divine light), as pervading everything from the elements like water to the sacred "Word" and even the perfected physical body.

translit: ātavāta vētakīta vātavāta vātiyē cūtavāta pātanāta cūtajāta jōtiyē.
translation: O primordial debater of all debates within the Vedic songs! O Lord of the sacred feet, beyond the illusion of debate! O Jothi, born of wonder!
commentary: God is the source of all philosophical arguments within the holy scriptures, yet is also the truth that lies beyond all intellectual debate. The final experience is a sense of wonder at the divine Jothi (light).

translit: aṅkacaṅka maṅkaipaṅka ātiāti ātiyē tuṅkapuṅka aṅkaliṅka jōtijōti jōtiyē.
translation: O most primordial of the primordial, who has as a part the woman with whom you are united in body! O pure, excellent body-Linga! O Jothi of Jothi, O Jothi!
commentary: God is the origin of all, containing both masculine and feminine energies in one united form. This divine body is a sacred form, or Linga, and is an expression of Jothi (divine light), the light that illuminates all other lights.

translit: attamutta attamutta ātiāti ātiyē cuttacitta captanirtta jōtijōti jōtiyē.
translation: O Father, Perfected One! O Father, Perfected One! O Primal Origin of all origins! O Jothi of Jothis, the sound-dance of pure consciousness!
commentary: The universe is a living performance. Vallalar describes this as the "sound-dance of pure consciousness," where the primal Jothi (divine light) expresses itself as the vibration and movement that constitute all of existence.

translit: añcalañcal eṉṟuvanteṉ neñcamarnta kuḻakaṉē vañcanañcam uṇṭakaṇṭa maṉṟuḷniṉṟa aḻakaṉē.
translation: O Youthful One who came saying, "Fear not, fear not," and settled in my heart! O Beautiful One who stands in the sacred hall, your throat having consumed the treacherous poison!
commentary: God came saying, "Fear not, fear not," and settled in Vallalar's heart. The same God, standing in the Hall, holds in His throat the poison that would have destroyed the worlds. The Protector who swallows poison for all is the same One who calms the fear of a single heart.

translit: toṇṭarkaṇṭu kaṇṭumoṇṭu koṇṭuḷuṇṭa iṉpaṉē aṇṭaraṇṭam uṇṭaviṇṭu toṇṭumaṇṭum aṉpaṉē.
translation: O Bliss that devotees see and see, scoop up, take, and consume within! O Loving One whom even Vishnu, who consumed the universe of the gods, throngs to serve!
commentary: Devotees see God again and again and drink the bliss within. Even Vishnu, said to have swallowed the universe, crowds to serve this loving Lord. The verse sets the greatest of the gods beside the humble devotee, and both are servants of the same love.

translit: kantatonta pantacintu cintavanta kālamē entaenta cantamuntu mantavanta kōlamē.
translation: O Time that came to shatter the bonds of attachment and conflict! O Form that came, advancing and slowing with every possible rhythm!
commentary: God is addressed as a power that shatters our inner bonds of attachment and a presence whose very form is the rhythm of the universe. The verse praises the divine for both liberating the soul from its limitations and being the beautiful, dynamic pulse of all existence.

translit: eṉṟumeṉṟiṉ oṉṟumaṉṟuḷ naṉṟuniṉṟa īcaṉē oṉṟumoṉṟum oṉṟumoṉṟum oṉṟateṉṟa tēcaṉē.
translation: O Isa, my One who always stands perfectly in the sacred hall! O Radiant Guru, who taught that the many, many things are all One!
commentary: God is both the perfect, singular presence in the sacred hall (maṉṟu, the inner space of consciousness) and the great teacher who reveals a core truth: all the seemingly separate things in the world are One. This verse celebrates the divine as both an intimate presence and the source of ultimate wisdom.

translit: eṭṭaeṭṭi oṭṭaoṭṭum iṭṭatiṭṭa kīrttiyē aṭṭavaṭṭam naṭṭamiṭṭa ciṭṭavaṭṭa mūrttiyē.
translation: O Fame that is the desired goal, reaching the unreachable to make it one! O Form of the circle of the perfected, who danced in the eight directions!
commentary: God is portrayed as the ultimate spiritual goal, the one who closes the gap between the soul and the seemingly unreachable divine. This divine power is a living dance that fills the entire cosmos, witnessed by the perfected beings who have realized the truth.

translit: cērikāra cāravāra cīrakāra ūraṉē ōrukāra tēratīra vāravāra tūraṉē.
translation: O Lord of the glorious city of Akāra, joined with the splendor of Ikāra! O Hero on the unique chariot of Ukāra, the Distant One who comes and comes!
commentary: This verse praises God through the fundamental sounds of creation, identifying the divine with the components of the sacred syllable AUM. Akāra ('a'), Ikāra ('i'), and Ukāra ('u') are seen as the primal vibrations of being. By addressing God this way, Vallalar points to the divine as the very sound-structure of reality.

translit: veyyanoyya naiyanaiya meypukaṉṟa tuyyaṉē aiyaraiya naiyumvaiyam uyyaniṉṟa aiyaṉē.
translation: O Pure One who spoke the Truth, causing the cruel and the worthless to be utterly crushed! O Lord of lords, O Master who stands so the suffering world may be saved!
commentary: God plays two vital roles: destroying falsehood with uncompromising Truth and saving the suffering world with compassion. The divine is a gentle savior and a fierce force for purity that cannot tolerate cruelty or illusion. In the end, that power serves the compassionate purpose of saving all beings.

translit: pācanāca pāpanāca pātatēca īcaṉē vācavāca tācarnēca vācakāca pēcaṉē.
translation: O Lord whose feet are a sacred realm, destroyer of bondage, destroyer of sin! O Fragrance itself, friend to your devotees, speaker of the flawless Word!
commentary: God's feet are a sacred place where bondage (pācam) and sin are destroyed. God is fragrance itself, the friend of devotees, the speaker of the flawless Word. The verse plays with sound, as the whole song does, so that the praise itself delights.

translit: uriyaturiya periyaveḷiyil oḷiyiloḷicey naṭaṉaṉē piriyaariya piriyamuṭaiya periyaritaya paṭaṉaṉē.
translation: O Dancer who is Light within light in the great expanse of the true Turīya (the fourth state of consciousness)! O One inscribed on the hearts of the great ones who possess a love from which it is impossible to part!
commentary: God dances as Light within light in the great expanse of the true fourth state (turiyam). The same God is written into the hearts of the great ones whose love can never be parted from Him. The highest state of consciousness and the deepest love meet in one Dancer.

translit: akilapuvaṉa uyirkaḷtaḻaiya apayamutavum amalaṉē ayaṉumariyum araṉummakiḻa aruḷumnaṭaṉa vimalaṉē.
translation: O pure one who grants refuge so that the lives of all worlds may flourish! O stainless one who graces us with the dance, delighting Brahma, Vishnu, and Siva!
commentary: God's dance is an act of universal grace that makes all life possible. Vallalar places this dancing Lord above even the great trinity of Brahma (the creator), Vishnu (the preserver), and Siva (the destroyer), suggesting a supreme reality that delights and harmonizes all other divine forces.
